en: The *Śrīmad-mīlana-tantra*, which is the principal [work], consists of the mantras accomplished through the threefold lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); it is the Blessed One, comprising both mundane and supramundane mantras, who has arisen from those mantras accomplished through the threefold lack of intrinsic nature. That tantra is the *Śrīmad-mīlana*; by way of its primacy, it is the Blessed One, the mundane and supramundane. [1b1 (D148b5, P371a2)]
Homage to Kurukullā!
Having bowed to the noble Nāgārjuna, who attained the first bhūmi,
we compose this commentary titled *Yogimanoharā* (Delighting the Minds of Yogins) on the *Krama*.
Having observed that the word of the Noble One is authoritative, this mere summary of my treatise is written; it should always be held in the hearts of people.

Indeed, in this context, within the *Śrī-samāja* and other tantras, all the verses exist in a highly dispersed manner. Taking them up, the venerable Ārya-Nāgārjuna—his heart overcome by compassion and observing the world of dull-witted people—desiring to compose the *Piṇḍīkrama* according to the sequence of the *Pañcakrama*, like a musician following thirty-two melodic threads (*sūtra*), spoke the following, beginning with a salutation, in order to establish the subject matter which is the nature of the fruit:
"Free from the conduct of the three worlds," and so forth.
The state that is common to the three worlds is the "threefold world" (*trilokī*); *triloky* itself is *trailokyam*, with the suffix *ṣyañ* added in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*).
It is also called *traidhātukaṃ*.
[It refers to] the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.

Regarding the sentient beings who exist therein, conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is precisely the adherence to the reality of the five aggregates and so forth as being solid and substantial. That itself is conduct (*ācāra*) and conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). "Free from" (*mukta*) means devoid of that. One might ask: what is its nature? Is it the nature of ultimate consciousness (*pāramārthika-vijñāna*)? To negate that, he says:

"Equal to space" means that his gnosis has gone to what is equal to space. Now, one might object: "In that case, because of the absence of all apprehension, does it not follow that there is nihilism? To refute this for those who have fallen into the precipice of the view of clinging to emptiness, [the text states]: "Emptiness is not other than things, nor is there the existence of things. In short, the intrinsic nature of all categories such as form and so forth is the self-nature of all things.

It is pure because it is free from the obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration of the knowable; or, as it is stated in scripture: "For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, these [emanations] flash forth from the pure Dharma-body."
It is peaceful (*śānta*), because it has the characteristic of the subsiding of all suffering, or because it is endowed with the flavor of peace (*śāntarasa*).
It is solitary,
because it is free from the conceptualization of existence and nirvāṇa;
it consists of supreme auspiciousness.
Because its nature is eternally arisen,
it is for this very reason the bringer of excellence.
The reality-nature of non-arising is accessible only to the minds of yogins through their emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
For this very reason, it is inaccessible to the śrāvakas and others;
it is difficult to understand and supremely profound because its intrinsic nature is the singular bliss of suchness.
Thinking that it is "difficult to investigate" because it cannot be analyzed or established even through suffering;
and that it is "most beneficial to oneself and others" because it is engaged in the ultimate welfare of both oneself and others—
by this, the accomplishment of one's own welfare is also expressed as being pervasive.
Because he thus manifests everywhere within the mental continuums of those to be trained;

"signless" (*nirnimitta*) refers to that in which the signs of heat (*ūṣman*) and so forth have completely subsided or vanished. Alternatively, because the mind is stabilized instantaneously without an external cause due to its natural flow, he emanates a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); this is the "signless. I pay homage—that is, I bow—to his "body," meaning his physical form. As for "of whom?"—it is indicated by the plural number, "of the Victors" (*jinānām*).
I pay homage to the body of the five Tathāgatas; why? Because it is recited in the *Samāja* Tantra.
It is bliss (*sukha*) because its nature consists of the four voids (*catur-śūnya*). It is "unequaled" (*asama-sama*) because it is beyond all comparison.
It is equal to the peerless universal emptiness because it has that as its intrinsic nature;
or alternatively,
the Buddhas are peerless, and it is equal to— that is, similar to— them.

Therefore, he whose singular form is non-conceptual— where "non-conceptual" means being free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and "singular" means peerless— and whose form is adorned with the thirty-two major marks and so forth.
Now, in order to state the purpose of the subject matter for this designation, he says "Śrīmān" and so forth.
A *piṇḍa* is the gathering together of many verses of the tantra into a single collection; because of its smallness, it is a *piṇḍī*, and its *krama* is the sequential arrangement.

I shall speak—that is, I shall explain—that which brings about the welfare of all sentient beings; for it is that in which there arises (*udaya*), that is, the exalted attainment (*abhyudaya*), of Buddhahood, which is the desired welfare of all the worlds.
Thus it is so.
In order to distinguish it from other tantras, he says:
"Of the Śrīmat Samāja Tantra.
*Samāja* means assembly (*samājanam*).
The single union of the thirty-two deities,
as well as that of emptiness and compassion; and it is said in the *Samājottara*:
"Assembly" (*samāja*) is said to mean "gathering" (*melana*), which is the designation for all Buddhas.
It is "glorious" (*śrīmat*) because that worldly and supramundane prosperity (*sampad*) exists within it; thus, it is the *Śrīmat-tantra*.
The analysis of the compound is: "the *Samāja-tantra* is that glorious [tantra] characterized by a composition of written texts."
Because that is difficult to understand, [it is said]:

"From the realization of the meaning of the six alternatives; from the realization of the interpretable, the definitive, the intentional language, and the non-intentional. Since the meaning of the six alternatives itself is not understood, for that purpose, the very same meaning of the six alternatives which has been explained by us in the commentary *Śrīmatsamājatantrapradīpodyotana* is here introduced.

The Jina speaks with intentional meaning (*neyārtha*) for those of ill fortune who are obscured; he speaks again with definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) for the sake of revealing the reality of things as they truly are. That which reveals the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to beings of superior inclination by means of seemingly contradictory discourse is called "speech of intentional terminology" (*saṃdhyāyabhāṣita*). Furthermore, regarding the mandalas and so forth, as well as in the conduct (*caryā*), that which explains the meaning in a clear and straightforward manner according to the circumstances is "speech according to the literal expression" (*yathārutabhāṣita*).

Words such as *koṭākhyaka* and others are excluded from both worldly usage and the [orthodox] scriptures; they are proclaimed to be the conventions (*saṃketa*) of the Tathāgatas and not ordinary speech (*anṛta*).

For the sake of awakening beings with dull faculties, the clear exposition of reality is declared to be "non-oblique" (*nāsandhya*). Within this commentary on the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*), which is captivating to yogins, a practitioner of moderate capacity should understand that there are two types of exegesis according to the distinction between the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
By this, the purpose of the subject matter has been stated.

Keeping in mind that its purpose is the removal of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), through which the attainment of the fruit occurs, [the author] says "the latent impression of conceptual construction" (*vikalpavāsanā*) and so forth;

the analysis of the compound is as follows: it is both a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which is an adherence to various and manifold false notions imposed upon the mind—and a latent impression (*vāsanā*).
The defects of false teachings and latent tendencies—
what indeed are they like?
They are those which cause delusion for the three worlds.
The wise one, the yogin, having thoroughly observed—that is, having seen—says for this very reason: "One should purify by means of the Yoga-tantra.

Yoga is Mahāvajradhara, whose nature is the union of wisdom and method (prajñopāya-samāpatti) in yuganaddha; that [tantra] in which he is expounded and elucidated is the Yoga-tantra. By that [means], one [purifies] the defects of the mind.
One should purify;
one should cultivate familiarity with one's own true nature.
And it is said in the scripture of the Sage: "The thorough knowledge of existence itself is called nirvāṇa."
He describes the conduct of the yogin: "The five desires," and so forth.

"Five desires" (*pañcakāmāḥ*) means the five things that are desired; they are called *kāma* because they are craved or longed for by the world—namely, the objects of the senses such as form, sound, and the rest.
One should not abandon them, nor leave them behind; nor should one afflict them with austerities (*tapas*).
By "austerities" is meant difficult practices, restrictive observances, and intense vows that do not rely on other vehicles (*anyayāna*).

The meaning of these terms, such as "difficult practices," is explained as follows: the performance of monastic duties and so forth through the application of bodily exhaustion constitutes "difficult practices."

The twelve ascetic practices (*dhūtaguṇa*), such as dwelling at the foot of a tree and so forth, are the observances (*niyama*). [Practices] such as leaping from mountains, entering fire, and the like are intense. While practicing these, one should not cause suffering;
if one is tormented, one does not achieve success and does not attain awakening (*bodhi*).

Therefore, having understood this, the yogin should not let the king of the mind become afflicted by suffering. If one asks, "Then how? he says: One should accomplish awakening—that is, Buddhahood—precisely through the bliss of enjoying the five objects of desire.
Why?
Because it follows the Yoga Tantra;
"Yoga Tantra" refers to the *Śrī-samāja*, and [this work] follows that tantra.
"From the realization of that object.

And it is said in another tantra: "By means of difficult and intense observances, the body withers; being pained, the mind becomes distracted; from distraction, there is no accomplishment—otherwise [it is achieved].
"By that," and so forth.

In this context, through that very enjoyment of the five objects of desire—form and so forth—as previously described, the practitioner remains established in restraint (*saṃvara*); because he cannot be disturbed by anything, this yogin who observes the vow is "indestructible" at all times. Regarding the phrase "the accomplishment of the vajra of body, speech, and mind":

although the *Piṇḍīkrama* (Summary Stage) indeed contains the meaning of the five stages within it, nevertheless, in the *Piṇḍīkrama*, the isolation of the object (*kāryaviveka*) is taught as the primary [subject].
The question is: how is the practice of the three vajras established here? [The answer is:

It is true that when the isolation of body (*kāyaviveka*) has been explained, the presentation of speech and mind follows; for there is no other form of mind apart from itself. The body emanated by the mind is indeed the mind, because it is the support of the mind; this is a matter of conventional linguistic usage.
Speech itself is the mind;
by this, their inseparable connection is indicated.
And it is said in the Tantra: "May you generate the mind in the form of the body, the body in the form of the mind, and the mind through the utterance of speech."

He states the place for accomplishing the siddhi of Vajradhara: in regions of a great forest (*mahāṭavī*), that is, in excellent locations because they are delightful due to the presence of bodies of water and so forth, and being adorned with fruits, flowers, and the like; on a mountain in a secluded spot; even in such a solitary place, one should accomplish—that which is to be realized—the "Compendium of All Siddhis" (*sarvasiddhisamuccaya*), in which all mundane and supramundane siddhis are collected and subsumed. That "Compendium of All Siddhis" is Buddhahood.

Alternatively: Through the application of the conceptualization of space, the aggregates (skandhas) are considered a great forest. By means of abiding in the non-abiding, in this vast abode of a single location—this wish-fulfilling tree of enjoyment, beautifully blossomed with various accomplishments and resplendent with the fruit of emanation, upon the mountain of perfect enlightenment, delightful and solitary due to its lack of intrinsic nature—one should practice that which is designated as "Vajra."

The meaning of this teaching is as follows: from the words "In space" up to "is considered a great forest," he provides an explanation of suchness (*tathatā*). In that context, the conceptualization of the aggregates and so forth is the arising of the aggregates;
because they are associated with that [conceptualization], the aggregates and so forth are considered a "great forest."

"The great forest is well-known, like space"— thus, because Vajrasattva and so forth are to be accomplished by relying upon the ordinary aggregates and so on, which are the locus for the cultivation of the ordinary aggregates and so on, the section beginning with "not a locus" and ending with "the great abode" is explained as another locus for the practice, consisting of the nature of clear light (*prabhāsvara*).

For one who has arisen from the state of the enjoyment-body (*sambhogakāya*), the description of the enjoyment [body] begins with "enjoyment" and so forth, up to "well-flowered. Furthermore, beginning with "emanation" (*nirmāṇa*) and ending with "the entire world," he states the locus for the practice of the emanation-body, which is the means for attaining perfect enlightenment.
The Teacher explains the purification of all things in the passage beginning with "niḥsvabhāva" and ending with "vajrasaṃjñakam.

First, in a place agreeable to the mind, facing east, one should sit upon a soft and comfortable seat in the sattvaparyaṅka posture and cultivate the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*), thinking: "I am the glorious Saṃāja."

Thereafter, having visualized a vajra produced from the syllable *hūṃ* upon the sun at one’s own heart, and again the syllable *hūṃ* atop that vajra, one should draw forth the Blessed One—the aforementioned wheel of gnosis—by means of masses of light rays from that seed-syllable shaped like hooks; having visualized him in the sky before oneself, one should first offer the water for honor (*arghya*).

Having worshipped with the flowers and other offerings emanated from that very seed-syllable, and having performed the prostrations, confession of misdeeds, and so forth, one should generate a mind of loving-kindness and the rest, whose nature is the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), toward all sentient beings. Immediately thereafter, the practitioner, having removed the ordinary ego through the liberation of emptiness, [visualizes] himself instantly...

One should meditate upon the form of Mahāvajradhara: white in color, two-armed, one-faced, seated upon a lotus and moon throne, resplendent with a halo of light, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, embraced by Vajradhātvīśvarī, and possessing a body that is like an illusion. This meaning is now declared by way of explanation according to the method of the *Jñānapradīpavajrasamādhi*. [The term] "jñā" functions in the sense of awakening (*avabodhana*), not in the sense of negation. That in which there is the absence of non-awakening is "jñāna. What is that?
Ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is inexpressible; because it overcomes all splendors by illuminating infinite world-systems, it is a lamp, and because it is indivisible, it is a vajra.

Then, by this sequence, having instantly visualized in one’s own heart the Vajra of Hatred (Dveṣavajra) of the form to be described, together with one’s own vidyā, through the passion of great desire; having caused it to melt and expanded it into the center of the lotus via the path of the avadhūtī; then, having projected it outward with the mantra *vajradhṛk* and visualized it in the form of Akṣobhya—having seen him as oneself, with a black face, three faces, and six arms—one should again cause him to enter into one’s own body according to the principle of milk and water. One should then contemplate oneself as having the color of a sapphire, slightly fierce and terrifying with bared fangs, with a body like that of a lord, embraced by a consort whose touch is like a vajra and whose body is like an illusion, seated upon a solar disc in the form of Dveṣavajra, consisting of the nature of the three sattvas. Thus, the mantra-practitioner abides in the samādhi of Dveṣavajra.

Immediately following this, adopting the intention of the *Vajrasattvasādhana* composed by the master Candrakīrti, one should contemplate the protection of the site; according to this sequence, the procedure therein is as follows: having uttered a long *HŪṂ*, one should emanate the ten wrathful deities, such as Yamāntaka and the rest, produced from that [syllable], standing upon solar discs in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, and endowed with the hand-symbols and so forth to be described hereafter, and contemplate them at the forefront of the mandalas of the ten directions.
And it is said in the Tantra: "The wrathful deities, born from the abode of hatred, are constantly intent on slaying;
they are accomplished for the purpose of slaying by the practitioner who possesses the supreme dharma. This is the meaning of this teaching:
the wrathful deities are Yamāntaka and the others; the abode of hatred is the syllable *HŪṂ*.

Those born from that [seed-syllable] are perfected by it; they are intent on slaying and are foremost in the rites for subduing the wicked. For the purpose of slaying obstacles through fierce rites, they succeed and accomplish their intended goal—[the goal] of one who possesses the supreme dharma, yet whose nature is exceedingly haughty.

"For the sake of destroying all obstacles," and so forth. Visualizing King Sumbha below, and having emanated and brought forth a second King Sumbha who stands before him in the form of a servant (*kiṃkara*) seeking an order, one should give the command with the wrathful form by means of this mantra of four *hūṃ*s: "Dveṣavajra, being enraged, [give the command]."

Thereafter, Sumbharāja, having received the command, went to the ten directions and pierced Indra and the other lords of obstacles in the heart with the hook (*aṅkuśa*), drew them forth, bound them by the neck with the noose (*pāśa*), and brought them back. Having entrusted them to the ten Wrathful Kings (*krodharāja*) and standing once more before [the central deity], Niṣumbharāja looks downward; the sequence of the colors, hand-symbols (*cihna*), and so forth of the second Sumbharāja and the lords of obstacles he has brought is now described. The sequence therein is as follows: one should visualize Indra, situated in the eastern direction, yellow, thousand-eyed, two-armed, single-faced, holding a *vajra* in a playful manner with his right and left hands, wearing a jewel crown, mounted upon the white elephant Airāvata, and being presented to Yamāntaka.

Likewise, in the western [direction] of Padmāntaka is Varuṇa, white, with one face and two arms, holding a serpent-noose playfully with his right and left hands, and mounted upon a dark-green tortoise.

Thus, to the north of Vighnāntaka is Kubera, yellow in color, mounted on a man, corpulent, with one face and two arms; he holds a mongoose in his right hand and a citron in his left, and wears a jeweled crown.

Thus, to the south of the immovable fire is Pāvaka, who is stout, adorned with red flames, red in color, and four-armed; he holds the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and a rosary (*akṣamālā*) in his right hands, and a staff (*daṇḍa*) and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his left hands, and is seated upon a goat.

Thus, in the southwest of Ṭakkirāja is [the deity] Kṛṣṇa: one-faced, two-armed, naked, deformed, with a mouth terrifying with fangs, a Rākṣasa with disheveled hair, holding a flaying knife in the right hand and a skull-cup in the left, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture upon a corpse seat.
Thus, in the northwest of Nīladaṇḍa is Anila, who is dark green, with one face and two arms, holding a wind-cloth, wearing a jewel crown on both [hands], and seated upon a yellow deer.

Likewise for Mahābala: in the northeast is Īśvara, white, with one face and two arms; holding a *ḍamaru* drum in the right hand and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff in the left; wearing matted hair, a bone necklace, and the moon, and mounted upon a bull. Likewise for Uṣṇīṣacakravartin: above is Pitāmaha (Brahmā), stout and yellow, with four faces and two arms; holding a rosary and a triple-staff (*tridaṇḍa*) in his right and left hands respectively; dwarfish, wearing a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), having matted hair, and having a swan as his vehicle.

Thus, below Sumbharāja is the Earth goddess: yellow, with one face and two arms, seated upon a lotus, holding a vessel of grain [in her left hand], and carrying a water-pot in her right; she wears a jeweled crown. [Then follows the section beginning with] "Vajrāmṛtamahārāja" and so forth. When the practitioner gazes [upon the mandala], then Amṛtakuṇḍalin is established as the second emanation at the northern gate. After that, one should visualize him in the form of the ten stakes, starting from "dark blue like the petal of a blue lotus" and ending with "having three faces and six arms"; all these are the specific attributes of Amṛtakuṇḍalin from the very beginning. This is clear.
"Then," and so forth: one should visualize that [the nails] are driven into the heads of the ten lords of obstacles, reaching down as far as the soles of their feet.

"With a vajra-hammer in hand," and so forth: having emerged in the form of Sumbharāja, one should meditate on him striking with the hammer given by Yamāntaka, or else with a hammer fashioned from his own emblem, while reciting the mantra *oṃ gha gha gha gha*, etc.
At the very moment of the striking, by means of the vajra-stake and the vajra-hammer strike, one should [visualize] Indra and his retinue being completely enveloped by the blazing vajra-fire.
One should consider those who have fled as wicked.

"Being burned here and there"—by this, having pinned down the ten directions, one should then preside over that which is below and above. With the four syllables *Ṭakki hūṃ jaḥ*, one should visualize outside, in sequence and according to their square and other shapes, the fourfold enclosure of iron, water, fire, and wind. Above that, one should meditate on a vajra-cage with the syllable *Bhrūṃ*, armor with the three syllables, and the ground consisting of a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) with the syllable *Hūṃ*. Thereafter, since emptiness alone is the supreme protection in the ultimate sense, one should enter the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) according to the meaning of the verse beginning with "non-existence" (*abhāva*). When all things, both stable and moving, are non-existent, there is the non-existence of meditation; because of the non-existence of meditation, there is the non-existence of the object of meditation.

"Cultivation is indeed not cultivation," because even that cultivation of what exists is non-existent due to its being present even without cultivation. Thus, that entity which is joined with existence and non-existence would not exist; therefore, the object of cultivation (*bhāvya*), the cultivator (*bhāvaka*), and the act of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) are not perceived. Alternatively, in ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), there is an absence of cultivation because of primordial purity (*ādiśuddhatva*). As for that cultivation whose nature is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), it too is not cultivated because it is [merely] a truth.
In this manner, an entity consisting of the two truths would not be something to be cultivated (*bhāvya*).

Since liberation occurs through the mere vision of the non-duality of the two truths, for those who have attained the stage of the simultaneous union (*yuganaddha*), this adherence to the notions of "the cultivator," "the cultivation," and "the object to be cultivated" is no longer perceived; it does not exist. By this, the emptiness of all things, such as the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*) and so forth, has been explained.

Then, by the power of previous vows, for the sake of arising [from meditative absorption], one should first produce the foundation mandala according to the sequence of the arising of existence (*bhavotpatti*). And it is stated in the *Vyavastholi*: "The meditation on the arising of the three vajras, preceded by the production of the *ālaya*, must be performed. This refers to the consecration and production of the ground of gnosis (*jñānabhūmi*); thus, "the production of the ground of gnosis" is said. One should meditate on the wind mandala situated in the middle of the space element, and so forth. It is produced from the two seed-syllables *hūṃ*. The syllable *yaṃ* is placed between two *hūṃ*s; there, the wind mandala is transformed by that *yaṃ*. "The wind mandala is joined with two vajras" means it is marked by two vajras produced from two *hūṃ*s on its sides. In this same way, it should be understood by the wise regarding the other three mandalas as well. Through the dissolution of the four mandalas, there is the "vajra-ground portion mandala"; the meditator should meditate on the vajra-made ground portion as the result of the dissolution of the four mandalas. Alternatively, through the transformation of the vajra residing in the four mandalas beginning with wind, there is a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) upon the earth mandala. Some write the "arising of phenomena" (*dharmodaya*) in the space element. In its center, upon the pericarp of a double-lotus, the meditator should visualize the ground portion consisting of a double-vajra, having dissolved the mandalas of wind and so forth produced from *yaṃ* and the other syllables. Therein, in the center of the double-vajra pedestal, the practitioner should meditate on a white syllable *bhrūṃ*, whose nature is Vairocana, which—through its transformation—becomes a celestial palace (*kūṭāgāra*) endowed with qualities such as being square, transparent, like an illusion, and provided with seats such as the moon and sun atop a double-lotus. As it is said in the Tantra: "The city of all Tathāgatas is endowed with mandalas such as the transparent one. Within this, without a seed-syllable, one should instantly meditate upon oneself in the form of the Great Vajradhara with three faces and so forth, surrounded by the deities of the mandala such as Vairocana; this is the visualization (*adhimokṣa*). This is the causal mandala (*hetumaṇḍala*).

Furthermore, by means of the *sampuṭa-yoga* (the yoga of union), and so forth, one should cause those who abide in the causal maṇḍala—the thirty-two deities by nature—to enter into one’s own body-maṇḍala through the *advaya-yoga* (the yoga of non-duality); this is the meaning. Furthermore, those Buddhas who have entered the body.

Having reflected upon the intrinsic nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and having dissolved them according to their respective places by means of the ultimate wheel— since they have merged into the maṇḍala circle—

one should cause them to enter sequentially into suchness, the clear light, by means of the verse beginning with "situated in the aggregate of form" (*vakṣyamāṇa-rūpaskandha-gata*), and by means of the verse beginning with "one should kill," one should render them devoid of intrinsic nature through the nature of emptiness.

This belongs to the Tathāgata; what is this "Tathāgata-array"? The intended meaning is the maṇḍala of the circle of deities residing within the body-maṇḍala. By means of this, the wise one shall attain—that is, obtain—the accomplishment characterized by Mahāmudrā, which is exceedingly distinguished.

Regarding the phrase "the aggregate of form" (*rūpaskandha*) and so forth: the aggregate of form is Vairocana; he is the Mirror-like [Wisdom] and has the nature of mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). The earth element (*bhūdhātu*), which has the nature of solidity, is Locanā. The eye faculty is Kṣitigarbha. Form is Rūpavajrā, conjoined with the Wrathful One. Together with Yamāntaka, who is of the same lineage as the Wrathful One, and Acala, these three—along with the fifth, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*)—proceed. In this manner, the yogin should infer [the correspondences] everywhere throughout the other verses.
"Feeling," and so forth: the aggregate of feeling is Ratnasambhava; he is equanimity, and he has attained the wisdom of equanimity. The water element has the nature of fluidity.

Or: Māmakī; the auditory faculty is Vajrapāṇi; and sound is Śabdavajrā. [This is] accompanied by the two wrathful deities and joined with Prajñāntaka and Ṭakkirāja. Regarding "perception" (saṃjñā) and so forth: the aggregate of perception is Amitābha; it is the state of discernment and has the nature of the wisdom of discernment (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna). Hutabhuj is the fire element; Pāṇḍarā has that as her nature. The olfactory faculty is Khagarbha; and odor is Gandhavajrā. [This is] accompanied by the two wrathful deities and joined with Padmāntaka and Nīladaṇḍa. Even though the Bodhisattvas reside on other levels, they enter elsewhere because of the relationship between object and subject.

"The formative factors (*saṃskāra*)," and so forth: the aggregate of formative factors (*saṃskāraskandha*) is Amoghasiddhi, the performance of duty (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*), and he who has attained the gnosis of the performance of duty. Tārā is Māruta, whose nature is wind. The faculty of taste is Lokeśvara, and taste is Rasavajrā. "Endowed with the pair of wrathful deities" means accompanied by Vighnāntaka and Mahābala; "joined with the wrathful deities above and below" refers to the union of Uṣṇīṣa and Sumbharāja. The nature [of touch] is Sparśavajrā. By the word "appearance" (*ābhāsa*), Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra are included. Since they have the nature of the three gnoses beginning with light (*āloka*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) arrives together with Nature (*prakṛti*). It is absorbed into the body of the Blessed One Akṣobhya. As for "consciousness, however, is radiant" (*prabhāsvara*): the body of the Blessed One extends from the head down to the feet.

By the phrase "it has come to the heart," [the ego] is absorbed into emptiness through this sequence. By means of stating its synonyms, [terms such as] "nirvāṇa" and so forth are easily understood. According to the principle that "what is soft is not firm," one should make that ego-conception firm.

By the passage beginning with *om śūnyatājñāna* and so forth, the essential nature of this very [mandala] is described through verses such as *paramārthamaṇḍalam*. Having shown the emergence from the state of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) by a yogin who has entered luminosity after having washed away all the stains of the afflictions by means of the object of focus that is luminosity, [the text continues] with the passage beginning *mantramūrttiprayogeṇa*. The "application of the form produced by mantra" refers to the fourfold vajra-form generated and accomplished by means of the three-syllable mantra. Its meaning is as follows: first, the realization of emptiness; second, the gathering of the seed-syllable; third, the manifestation of the image; and fourth, the placement of the syllable. One should establish the connection with the visualization of the deity according to the sequence to be explained. The "space-element" is the mind itself, which is luminosity. From that arises the sun-mandala in the form of skillful means, transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*. Upon that, the practitioner—the yogin—visualizes the moon-disk transformed from the syllable *oṃ*. In the center of that moon-disk is an eight-petaled lotus of red color, transformed from the syllable *āḥ*. Above the pericarp of the lotus, in an ascending order, one should contemplate the three syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. Immediately following this, through the transformation of the sun and so forth, one should meditate upon the perfectly full moon-mandala as being nothing but mind, more clearly manifest, and having the nature of the light of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The one who cultivates the soft state: having internalized all things, both stationary and moving, within this very [state], one should make firm the jewel of one's own mind.

With the mantra beginning “Oṃ dharmadhātve” and so forth, it is said: “The meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of mere gnosis (*jñāna*) is designated as ‘yoga’”; thus is yoga. Furthermore, [the text] says “And again,” and so on: the yogin should contemplate three syllables upon a moon disc in the center of the moon. Through the transformation of these three syllables, there arises a white five-pronged vajra, which indicates the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*). Upon that vajra, one should again contemplate the three syllables, which are the gnosis of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), having the nature of the light-manifestation (*ālokābhāsa*). Through the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means, the form of the deity is born; according to the principle of the unsurpassed *sandhi*, one should contemplate oneself as the transformation of these two gnoses—the Saṃbhogakāya, resembling a white kunda flower or the moon, perceived through light, with two arms, one face, and the primordial form.

And it is said in the *Tattvasiddhi* by Nāgabuddhipāda: "One should meditate upon this goddess—who has two arms and one face—as a sublime deity, instantly, while staying in whatever place one pleases. Thus, if Vairocana and the others are intended to be meditated upon as the central lords (*nāyaka*), then the sequence is that one should first meditate on the wheel and so forth produced from their three syllables, and from that, the form of Mahāvajradhara. The commentary on the two verses beginning with "Akṣobhya" is to be understood following the ritual of placement (*nyāsa*). When the placement is being performed, for the sake of assuming the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) here at the beginning, one should effect the entry into the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth.

And so it is said in the Tantra: "The form of the Mahāpuruṣa empowered all the mantras of the Tathāgatas. As soon as they were empowered, that very Bodhicittavajra appeared to all the Tathāgatas in the form of three faces. Furthermore, it is said: "Just as the Lord of Jinas, established in the ten directions, does not have flesh, bone, or blood in his body, yet for the benefit of sentient beings he performs his activity through the *dhātu* by means of the *nirmāṇakāya*"; thus one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and so forth. The seed-syllable placement (*bījanyāsa*) from Vairocana down to Śumbha is to be understood according to its respective locations in the void. However, the locations for the seed-syllables and so forth are clear from the root text itself. Nevertheless, there is a distinction regarding the placement of Moharati and the others, as well as Lām, Mām, Pām, and Tām, who are the deities of the sense objects. Some write the seed-syllables as Jaḥ, Hūṃ, Vaṃ, and Hoḥ; their explanation must be considered. Why? Because in the Root Tantra, the seed-syllable is seen to be precisely the syllable of one's own name.

Therefore, one should assign the mantras beginning with *moharatī*, which serve as the seed-syllables (*bīja*), as having the nature of earth and the other elements according to the instructions of the Tantra. Likewise, the objects of the three types of form and so forth are also *Rūpavajrā* and the others. The question is: "How can there be an assignment (*nyāsa*) in the absence of the employment of these mantras? The answer is: "True; it will become clear in the *Mahāsādhana* by the passage beginning with 'by Kṣitigarbha and the others. Now follows the connection with the two previously mentioned verses concerning the entry into Akṣobhya. Then, regarding the passage beginning with "Then the assignment... and ending with "of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth in their proper order," everything has been explained by me according to the sequence of the text. By this, one becomes perfected in the body-maṇḍala; this is the *Atiyoga*. Now, he speaks in order to explain the *Mahāyoga*: "Situated in the center of the head," and so forth. Regarding "by means of the application of sovereignty": it occurs immediately after the recollection. The connection is as follows: one should visualize a moon-maṇḍala situated in the center of the head, the syllable *Oṃ* above that, and from that, Locanā and the various forms of the Body-Vajra (*Kāyavajra*). Regarding "in the middle of that," and so forth: it is easy to understand that one should visualize the Sovereign alone, who is the primary figure, in the midst of the Vairocana array. Regarding "bearing the body of the Buddhas," and so forth: the "Buddhas" are the Tathāgatas existing in the three times. One who bears their body because he is of the same nature as them is "Bearing the Body of the Buddhas. He in whom the glorious Locanā resides is "the Glorious One" (*Śrīmān*).

The "Three Vajras" refers to the Great Vajra-holder; through that state of indivisibility and identity, may he establish his station—that is, grant his empowerment—within my body. Regarding the term *kāyavajriṇaḥ*: the word *vajrin* is used in the singular despite the plural sense due to the archaic (ārṣa) usage. One should understand that this applies similarly to the other two verses as well. With this verse beginning with "In the ten directions," the practitioner should offer a prayer for the entire array of Vairocana. The same [procedure] applies to speech and mind as will be described below; the remainder is as before.

"Locanā," and so forth. Immediately after the prayer, the two arrays of deities enter into union with one another and experience the bliss of supreme joy (*paramānanda*). Then, having entered through the gateway of Vairocana in the form of a white fluid, they reach the stage of gnosis (*jñānabhūmi*), fulfill all desires, and satisfy [the practitioner]—thus one should contemplate. "That body," and so forth, up to "Oṃ"—this is the collective meaning: one should solidify the non-dual ego-identity (*advayāhaṃkāra*). In this way, for the consecrations of speech and mind, one should understand that entry into their respective places occurs respectively in the form of red and black fluids. "The tongue-lotus," and so forth, is clear from the very beginning. "Dharma," and so forth: Dharma is Amitābha; he is the "path of speech" because his nature is speech.
He is "Glorious" (Śrīmān) because he is joined with Śrī Pāṇḍarāvāsinī; "Trivajra," and so forth, is as before.

"Of Vajradharma," and so forth. Regarding the word *yat*: where *yā* would have been expected, it is used as *vācā* or *vācaḥ*. What kind of speech is it? It is *nirukti*, which means "etymological explanation"; that is the perfection (*sampat*). Those which possess this are the "perfections of etymological explanation" (*niruktisampadaḥ*). The mention of "etymological explanation" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), by which the perfections of Dharma, meaning, and eloquence (*pratibhāna*) are also included. Thus, it refers to such speech, such as *vācā* or *vācaḥ*. "Like a bearer of the Dharma" (*dharmadharopama*): this would be or they would be like a bearer of the Dharma. By this, it is intended that she is perfected through the utterance of all sounds without exception. "Having placed [it] in the heart," and so forth, is easy to understand. Therein: within the lunar disc, upon the seed-syllable (*bīja*) located on the hub (*varaṭaka*) of the vajra born from the syllable *HŪṂ*, there is again a five-rayed [seed-syllable].
Such is the traditional teaching.
The passage beginning with "tataḥ" and so forth is again easy to understand. Regarding "vajracittadhara" and so on:

*vajracitta* means the mind (*citta*) that is like a *vajra*; because it does not shrink from either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, Akṣobhya is the "Bearer of the Vajra-Mind" (*vajracittadhara*), as he maintains such a mind. He is "Glorious" (*śrīmān*) because of his union with Māmakī. The passage beginning with "trivajra" and so forth is as explained previously.
"Whatever is the mind of Samantabhadra, the Lord of the Guhyakas," and so forth.
"Guhyaka" refers to Vairocana and the others, who "proclaim" (kāyanti) or speak of the "secret" (guhyam), which is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*).
"Indra" means the lord (*indra*); thus, he is the lord of the Guhyakas, meaning he is the preeminent one among those who teach reality (*tattva*).
"Dhīmān" means one who possesses wisdom (*dhī*).

That wisdom is Sparśavajrā; he who possesses her is "Dhīmān. May the mind of such an Akṣobhya, and my own mind as well, become like that—resembling the Holder of the Vajra (*vajradhara*). Of him who resembles the Holder of the Vajra.
"Oṃ sarvatathāgatacitta... and so forth, up to "...one should contemplate the Samayasattva"; this [passage] is easy to understand from the root text itself.
"One should visualize the subtle Jñānasattva situated in the center of the heart," and so forth.

Having meditated upon the Jñānasattva—situated in the center of the heart, within the heart of the accomplished Samayasattva; subtle, the size of a barley grain, red in color, with two arms and one face, embraced by a consort of his own radiance, holding a vajra and a vajra-bell, seated upon a moon on a double lotus—one should place [the mantra] in his heart.

In his heart, upon a moon disc, one should visualize a vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*, within which is the syllable *hūṃ* encircled by *oṃ* and the other vowels; this is designated as the Samādhisattva.

In the same way, the yogin of Vairocana and the others should meditate on the syllable *oṃ* and so forth in the center of their own respective symbols, which are born from *oṃ* and the rest, situated upon their own seats born from *oṃ* and the rest.

Thereafter, one should again visualize Mahāvajradhara on the crown of the head, white in color, with two arms and one face, in union (*samputa-yoga*) with Vajradhātvīśvarī, delighting his entire body with streams of *bodhicitta* that radiate forth; this is the tradition of Mahāyoga.
By this, the fulfillment of one’s own welfare is declared.
Regarding the perfection of the welfare of others:
now one should begin the accomplishment of the mudrā,
starting with the words "Having obtained a maiden," and so forth.
She is called a *kanyā* because her form is desirable.

She is *viśālākṣī*, meaning she whose eyes are wide and consist of the two truths; this is a specific qualification of Mahāmudrā herself, described as "adorned with beauty and youth" and "dark like the petals of a blue lotus. Regarding the phrase "of the washerman": it means that for one who delights the members of the mandala—the disciples to be trained—through the gift of Dharma, she is the woman of his own family (*svakulāṅganā*).

Having taken hold of an external woman who is well-trained, auspicious, and consequently devoted and affectionate toward the practitioner—one distinguished by such qualities—and having placed her before him, he should remove her ordinary nature and visualize her as resembling the *jñānamudrā* to be described hereafter: single-faced, two-armed, and white in color.
For she is indeed such a *jñāna-aṅganā*;
she is the Great Goddess residing in the heart, the one who conveys the yoga for yogins, the mother of all Buddhas, known as Vajradhātvīśvarī.

Having ascertained the external and internal mudrās, one should place the seed-syllables of Vairocana, such as Oṃ and so forth, upon the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so on. However, there is a specific distinction here: having placed the wrathful queens born from the syllable Hūṃ upon the limbs such as the arms, and having meditated on the mudrās as being of one's own form through the entry of Sparśavajrā, one should perform embracing, kissing, and so forth with the pride of passion preceded by the consecration of the vajra and lotus. Then, intent on the utterance of the syllable Hūṃ, one should abide in the activity of the woman through the yoga of Amitābha.

Then, having clearly experienced the three cognitions beginning with light, and having exhorted all the Tathāgatas residing within one’s own body, one should emit the bodhicitta—which is the form of great bliss—through the opening of the vajra-mouth during the stage of emanation by means of the yellow *phaṭ* syllable mantra. Immediately thereafter, in the center of the lotus, with the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) of Amoghasiddhi, one should worship all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth residing within one’s own body by means of the Garuḍa-mudrā; as it is also stated in another tantra:
The nectar is to be taken with the tongue for the purification of one's own strength.

*Oṃ sarvatathāgata* and so forth; from the root [mantra] onwards, this is easily understood. Beginning with "Having meditated on the syllable *oṃ* at the crown of the head" and ending with "*oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjā*," I have explained everything according to the sequence of the root text. By means of this, up to the limit of the bliss of delight, there is the first samādhi, named the Supreme King of Samādhis (*samādhirājāgrī*).
Now, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others, the practitioner should emanate the maṇḍala circle by means of the generation stage of existence.
This is because it is explained in the *Vajramālāvyākhyātantra* that the emanation should be performed to the same extent as the placement of the limbs [of the deities].
"Produced from the syllables of one's own mantra," and so forth.
Its meaning is as follows:

having visualized within the center of the lotus of wisdom the form of the bodhicitta consisting of thirty-two seed-syllables, such as the syllable *hūṃ* and so forth, one's own [deity] is produced from that *hūṃ* syllable, which is the syllable of one's own mantra,
and is empowered by the three vajras.

The Mind-Vajra should manifest the form of Dveṣavajra, which consists of the three vajras and is empowered by one’s own body, speech, and mind. Alternatively, from the perspective of the Wisdom Consort (jñānāṅganā), since the actual emission of the bodhicitta does not occur, the mantrin should produce the thirty-two-deity maṇḍala-circle through the sole emanation of mantra. And it is said in the *Vyavasthāli*: "From the bodhicitta, by means of the sole emanation of mantra."
Regarding this, the word "ca" (and) is placed out of its sequential order.
One who holds the vajra that indicates the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*), such as that produced by the *vajradhṛk* mantra and so forth, is *Vajradhṛk*.
Alternatively, one who holds the vajra-wisdom (*vajrajñāna*) whose nature consists of the two truths is *Vajradhṛk*. By "mantra," the *utsarga-mantras* alone are indicated.
Regarding the phrase "accomplished by that":
why?

Because previously, within the lotus of wisdom, the syllable of one's own mantra was produced as the form of Akṣobhyavajrin; with reference to that, and by way of its detailed explanation, it is clearly stated that [the deity] is once again accomplished.
Therefore, the connection is that one should cause [the deity] to emerge outward from the heart—the womb of the deity—to be described below, by means of the mantra mentioned immediately prior.
In this way, the sequence of explanation beginning with "accomplished" (*niṣpanna*) and so forth regarding the mantras of the Jinas and Jinis to be described below should be understood by the wise.
As for what some write—that the syllables of one's own mantra are mantras such as *Vajradhṛk*, and by those [syllables], Akṣobhya and the others are accomplished—that is to be reflected upon.
Why?

Because, to the extent that the arrangement of the *vajradhrk* and other seed-mantras as well as the arrangement of the emission-mantras has been set forth [in the *Vyavasthālī*], it has been demonstrated by the venerable Nāgabuddhi.
Alternatively:
If it is precisely here, it is because of the statement: "Maitreya and Kṣitigarbha are produced from the Maimthlī mantra.
Regarding "Akṣobhyavajrin" and so forth, and "Dveṣavajrin" with "jaṭā" and so forth, the meaning is easy to understand.

Regarding the phrase "with Akṣobhya as his crest-ornament" (*akṣobhyakṛtaśekharam*), we shall provide an explanation for this term after the Jñānacakra described below; it has not been explained here by me because it is not relevant to the present context.
As for the phrase "resembling a whirlpool of kings" (*nṛpāvarttakasaṃkāśam*):
It resembles a royal turban; with faces that are black, red, and white— meaning that,
according to the appropriate application, it is adorned here by three faces representing the wrathful, the peaceful, and the great passion through the purity of the body.
"Complete with all ornaments" means because he wears the attire of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*);
"six-armed" means...
Because of the purity of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). Regarding the phrase "the vajra," etc.:

the symbols of the six Tathāgatas, such as the vajra and so forth, are held as being identical [to him] in order to demonstrate the nature of the six Tathāgatas, because he is the sovereign of the mandala; this is what is meant by this.

The meaning is that even those who provide explanations of the *Kṛṣṇapadma* must certainly reject [that view] according to the tradition of explaining the *Vyavasthāli* treatise composed by Ārya Nāgabuddhipāda and others; this, however, is a qualification of Dveṣavajra while residing in the womb of the goddess, and everything must be performed [in this manner].
The explanation from "having gazed" (*vyavalokya*) up to "sits before [her]" (*purato niṣīdati*) is very clear from the root text itself.
As for "having caused him to enter" (*anupraveśya tam*), etc.:
Having caused that Hatred-Vajra standing before one to enter through the path of Vairocana, one should meditate on the form of Hatred-Vajra within one's own heart-body;
its former form having been transformed into the form of Akṣobhya, it possesses the luster of a sapphire and is radiant because it is endowed with all jewels.

For this reason, one should meditate upon the Hatred-Vajra situated in the center of the solar disc: a black *hūṃ*-born vajra arising from a *hūṃ*-born sun, constantly manifesting like a great lamp, having the form of a mass of light for the purpose of dispelling the darkness of ignorance, known as the Samādhi-sattva, and joined with the seed-syllables of the five Tathāgatas—this is the traditional instruction. "The Hero embraced by his own mudrā" means the Hero embraced by Sparśavajrā.
The connection is as follows: by means of this, the yogin established in the *dveṣavajra-samādhi* should project the entire mandala beginning with Vairocana.
Regarding "Jinajik": one whose nature is to conquer is a *jina*; he conquers the Māras by means of the twelvefold Wheel of Dharma, and thus he is "Jinajik" (the Conqueror).
Alternatively: by means of the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*), he overcomes the four Māras;
[he is] the Conqueror with faces that are white, black, and red, and so forth. That very Blessed One sits upon a moon-disc in front; the connection is that "he caused him to sit."
"Ratnadhṛk" means he who holds the jewel that fulfills all aspirations; thus, he is Ratnadhṛk. Alternatively, he is Ratnadhṛk because he holds the jewel of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
That he has faces that are yellow, black, and white is easy to understand.

"Those who abide on the plane of ego-grasping" refers to those beings who are arrogant due to their wealth; having subdued them through generosity and established them on the plane of the purity of the purification of pride, he sits on the right side of the Blessed One.
"ĀROLIG": *ā* means "all around"; *roḥ* refers to *saṃsāra* (cyclic existence); because he emerges (*nirgacchati*) from that, he is ĀROLIK.
Alternatively, *āra* refers to the three knowledges; because he has gone beyond them to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), he is *Ārolika*.

Regarding the phrase "with red, black, and white faces," it is clear that from the use of the qualifying word "lotus" (*padma*) in the expression "opening by the hundreds [of petals] with the right [hand]," it is understood that the lotus itself is red. It is situated in the region of the heart.

"Prajñādhṛk" means that wisdom (*prajñā*), which has the characteristic of discernment (*pravicaya*), holds those [elements]; thus he is "the holder of wisdom. Alternatively, wisdom is the lunar light; he holds that in the sky by means of the subtle element (*sūkṣmadhātu*); thus he is "the holder of wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "with green, black, and white faces," and so forth, the six arms and the rest are easy to understand. As for "radiant with rays," this means it is endowed with blazing flames.
"For these families are indeed the accomplishers of liberation through the five desires.
These families, having the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), become accomplishers of liberation through the enjoyment of desire.

Furthermore, for the enjoyment of Vairocana and the others, he emits the four goddesses. Therefore, it says: "Delighting in delusion" (*moharatī*); "delusion" (*moha*) refers to Vairocana; in that [delusion].

"Delight" (rati) means delight in delusion (moha). Alternatively, "delight in delusion" (moharati) refers to delight in the purification of delusion. "One should create" (srjet) means one should bring [the deity] forth within the womb (garbha).

"Marked by Vairocana on the crown" means: how is this so? For since Locanā and the others are emanated by the Lord of the Mandala (cakreśvara), it would seem more appropriate for them to be marked by the Lord of the Mandala himself, according to the logic of father and son; and the father is indeed the Blessed One, the Sovereign of the Mandala, Mahāvajradhara. While it is true that the Blessed One is the sovereign even over the Lords of the Families (kuleśas), nevertheless, marking them by the Lords of the Families alone is proper, because if they were marked otherwise, success (siddhi) would not arise due to the incompatibility with the meditation on the distinct families. [The practitioner] should sit—that is, take his seat—in the eastern corner, which is the southeast (agnikoṇa).

Regarding "delight in hatred" (*dveṣarati*): hatred is Akṣobhya; delight in that is *dveṣarati*. Alternatively, delight in the purification of the affliction of hatred is *dveṣarati*. The phrases "with faces black, red, and white," and so forth, are easy to understand. Regarding "she sits upon the Nairṛta [direction]": why is no seat mentioned here? Because there is no fixed rule for Māmakī. When she is dependent on the Jewel Family (*ratnakula*), then there is a jewel-seat; but now, being dependent on the Vajra Family (*vajrakula*), there is only a sun-seat. Regarding "delight in passion" (*rāgarati*): passion is Amitābha; delight in that is *rāgarati*. The phrase "with faces red, black, and white," and so forth, is easy to understand.

Regarding "Vajraratī": Vajra is Amoghasiddhi; delight in him is Vajraratī. Alternatively, delight in vajra-wisdom is Vajraratī. The description of the green, black, and white faces, and so forth, is easy to understand.

In the second enclosure, however, the yogin should emanate Rūpavajrā and the others. It is called *rūpa* because it is manifested (*rūpyate*) or reflected; it is called *śabda* because it is sounded (*śabdyate*); it is called *gandha* because it is smelled (*ghrāyate*); it is called *rasa* because it is tasted (*rasyate*); and it is called *sparśa* because it is touched (*sprśyate*). Due to the word *vajra*, they are designated as Rūpavajrā and so forth because they are the purity of form and the other [sensory objects] through their respective samādhis. Now, for the sake of experiencing the objects such as form and the rest, there is the emanation of the four goddesses, Rūpavajrā and the others, by means of their own names. However, in this case, Śabdavajrā, because she is sealed by Ratnasambhava, is indeed Ratnāsana.

Likewise, regarding the third layer, on the front panel and so forth, the explanation of the passage beginning with "Samantabhadra and Kāśyapa" is as follows: there is the placement of the Bodhisattvas, such as Maitreya and Kṣitigarbha, who are produced from their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*), starting with the nature of the sense-fields (*āyatana*) of the eye and so on. Their seed-syllables are easily understood from the very beginning. Maitreya is so called because he takes all beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, and so on—as the object of his loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Kṣitigarbha is one whose internal essence (*garbha*) is a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) as immovable as the earth (*kṣiti*). Vajrapāṇi is one who holds (*dhārayati*) the vajra, which is the nature of the five wisdoms (*pañcajñāna*). Ākāśagarbha is one whose internal essence is the unobstructed wisdom that has reached the sky (*ākāśa*). Lokeśvara is the lord (*īśvara*) of the worlds through the power of his meditative absorption. Mañjuśrī is the beautiful glory (*śrī*) of the mind (*manas*) arising from the meditative absorption of radiant light (*prabhāsvaram*). Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin is one who completely obstructs (*viṣkambhayati*) the hindrances, which are afflictions (*kleśa*), by the power of the illusion-like meditative absorption (*māyopama-samādhi*). Samantabhadra is the auspicious (*bhadra*) one who is beautiful (*sobhana*) in every respect (*samanta*). Regarding the phrase "these have their own lords as crowns" and so forth: these aforementioned Bodhisattvas, Maitreya and the others, are intended to be sealed by their respective lords, Vairocana and the rest. They should be seen as being identical to them in terms of color and so on, being endowed with white and other colors. The phrase "by means of arms and weapons" and so forth—the word "and" (*ca*) here functions as a conjunction; the word "also" (*api*) implies the inclusion of their seats. The Bodhisattvas, Maitreya and the others, are equal to their respective presiding lords (*adhipati*); the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) is that this is because they have attained those same stages (*bhūmi*). As for the statement "Maitreya alone [carries] the right [hand]," and so forth: the meaning is that in the right hand, at the position of the wheel, he carries the *nāgapuṣpa* (dragon-flower).

The passage beginning with "saśodhyāyatane" and so forth is easy to understand; it refers to the emanation of the ten wrathful deities (*krodha*) by way of the nature of the limbs and other body parts, such as the arms. "Yamāntakṛt," "the origin of the mantra," and so forth [refer to] that which is beneath the earth.

Between these two textual fragments, "He stands" and "the end," there exist many specific epithets for the ten wrathful deities (*krodha*). Regarding some of those numerous epithets, I shall write a brief analysis following the *Ārya* [commentary]; that should be understood by a scholar of keen intellect. As for the other terms for which no explanation has been provided, they are easily understood upon seeing them in their original context. Yamāntakṛt: Yama is hell; because the Blessed One brings an end to—that is, destroys—that [hell] through the meditative absorption of Great Wrath (*mahākrodhasamādhi*), he is called Yamāntakṛt.

Alternatively: Yama is the essence of delusion (*moha*) and ignorance (*avidyā*); he brings an end to that through ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), thus he is Yamāntakṛt. Regarding the phrase "with black, red, and white faces," and so forth: the first face is black, the left face is red, and the right face is white. Because he stands in the eastern direction, he is seated at the eastern gate. Regarding the phrase "Prajñāntakṛt" and so forth: because he destroys the afflictions (*kleśa*) by means of wisdom (*prajñā*), he is Prajñāntakṛt.
Alternatively, he is called *Prajñāntakṛt* because he brings an end to that wisdom which consists of conceptual construction by means of its entry into luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).

Regarding the phrase "adorned with snakes" (*ahibhūṣaṇa*), this should be understood as a description applicable to all the wrathful deities (*krodha*) both mentioned and yet to be mentioned. He "stands in the southern direction" means that he is seated at the southern gate.
*Padmāntakṛt* means like a lotus that has been smeared with water.

Having become unstained by the afflictions (*kleśa*), he destroys them; thus, he is *Padmāntakṛt* (the Maker of the End of the Lotus). Alternatively, "lotus" (*padma*) refers to the womb (*yoni*); "end" (*anta*) means the middle. Within that, by means of the method of the union of the two organs, he produces—that is, generates—the bliss of supreme joy; thus, he is *Padmāntakṛt*.
Because he stands in the direction of Varuṇa, he is seated at the western gate.
“Vighnāntakṛt” and so forth: he is called Vighnāntakṛt because he brings about the end—that is, the destruction—of obstacles (*vighna*).

Alternatively, the four elements are “obstacles” because they afflict the body through their decrease and increase; he is called Vighnāntakṛt because he effects their destruction through the arising of the knowledge of skillful means (*upāyajñāna*).
“With faces blue, red, and white,” and so forth.
The meaning established by this convention— that the first face is blue, the left is red, and the right face is always white—
is indicated by the statement that he "stands in the direction of Kauravyā," meaning he is seated at the northern gate.
"Immovable" (*acala*) and so forth:
he brings about the realization (*nidhyapti*) through the Vajroṣṇīṣa-sādhana for those whose hearts are constantly agitated by the eight worldly concerns; thus he is "immovable.
"With the luster of sapphire" (*indranīlaprabha*) and so forth: just as there is the radiance or brilliance of a sapphire, in that same way [is he]. *Ṭakkirāja*.
Regarding the phrase "holding the Vajra-hūṃkāra-mudrā with two hands," it is said here:

having formed two fists according to the method of embracing Prajñā and so forth, one should extend both little fingers and interlace them, then extend both index fingers upward; after that, with both thumbs.
Having joined the two index fingers and ring fingers, it becomes the Vajra-hūṃkāra mudrā,
which is the Nīladaṇḍa.
He is called Nīladaṇḍa because he wields a blue staff (*daṇḍa*)— the punishment (*nigraha*)— against the sins of sentient beings.
"Stands in the direction of Vāyu" means he is seated in the northwest corner (vāyukoṇa).

"Of great power" (mahābala) means that by the power of ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), he crushes the secondary afflictions (upakleśa) of sentient beings; thus, he is Mahābala. "Uṣṇīṣacakra" means...
Because he bestows the knowledge of the transcendence of the three realms for the sake of sentient beings, he dwells in the Brahma-abode as the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, the King Sumbha.

Having summoned the hosts of obstructors from the ten directions, King Nisumbha performs the ritual of pinning and subduing them. Then, having emitted the entire mandala consisting of the thirty-two deities—beginning with the syllable *a*—and thus having emitted the mandala-circle composed of the three beings (*trisattva*), one should perform the practice of the entry of the wisdom-circle (*jñānacakra*), the empowerment, and so forth, according to this sequence. This is the sequence: having drawn the wisdom-circle into the sky before oneself by means of the rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart, and having seen it there, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, worship it, and [invite it] with the mantra *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*.

Having performed the drawing in, entering, and so forth according to the appropriate method, one should cause the wisdom-circle (*jñānacakra*) to enter the commitment-circle (*samayacakra*), like water mixing with milk. Then, in the same manner, having drawn in the five Tathāgatas— who hold vases filled with the water of wisdom— by means of the rays of light from the seed-syllable situated in one's own heart;

Having beheld Locanā and the other goddesses in the sky, the mantra-practitioner should request consecration. Thereupon, the five Buddhas recite the verse beginning with, “The great jewel of consecration,” and they bestow the consecration with sprouts of mango and other trees. At that very moment, the goddesses Locanā and the others perform an auspicious rite with verses of benediction.
Following the consecration, a rain of flowers falls and the sound of celestial drums resounds.
Subsequently, it should be understood that the head is marked by whichever family lord (kuleśa) serves as the seal for each of the thirty-two deities;
for has not the noble one indeed stated the sealing in the *Utsarga-maṇḍala*?
However—

In that very context, let it be heard: having attained the form of the complete deity who presides over the syllables (*akṣarābhimānin*), he spoke regarding the preservation of the tradition (*āmnāya*). Sealing [the body] is not well-suited to the intention of the Noble Ones; rather, the sealing that occurs immediately after the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is intended for this purpose.
Immediately following this, in order to explain the subtle yoga of the reality of the deity (*devatātattva-sūkṣmayoga*), he says, "At the tip of the nose, a mustard seed," and so forth.
One should contemplate a mustard seed—that is, a drop of semen—at the tip of one's own nose, within the aperture of the vajra.

This point was also taught with intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*) in a Mahāyāna sūtra: "On a single hair-tip there are many Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. And in the *Bhadracaryā*, it is also said:
"Upon a single atom are Buddhas as numerous as atoms, along with their sons."
"Seated in the center" means that,
alternatively,

one should visualize a vajra the color of a blue lotus and the size of a barley grain right there; likewise, the yogin of Vairocana and the others should contemplate what was just described at the tip of the nose— that is, at the tip of the goddess’s lotus-nose.
Alternatively,
there is the traditional teaching that one should visualize the marks of the wheel and so forth as being the size of a chickpea husk;
this is the "word of knowledge," which serves as the cause for supramundane gnosis.
Delightful like a rainbow because it is endowed with white and other colors;
secret,
being beyond the reach of others, and conceived through primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).

For one who meditates on the *piṇḍīkrama*, the great jewel arising from the five families—whose nature is mere gnosis (*jñānamātra*), which is five-colored, and so forth—is like a diamond or other insignia, as precious as a great gem. (30) *The Pañcakramatippanī* of Muniśrībhadra. (D164b1, P392b2) It is "like a jewel" because it is of great value, like a diamond and other such symbols.
By the words "the state of gnosis" (*jñānapada*) and so forth, the entire moving and non-moving world is to be qualified;

for this very reason it is said: "The vision of reality is established through yoga. One should meditate through the process of *samāpatti*. He states the fruit of this very meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in the passage beginning with "one should expand the stable jewel," and so forth.
When both the sign of vision (*darśananimitta*) and the sign of apprehension (*udgrahaṇanimitta*) arise—
therein, the sign of vision is the stability of the mind, and the sign of apprehension is the sign of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*).
Then, having recognized the vajra and so forth as immovable through meditative cultivation, one should emanate them for the sake of production by virtue of mastery over cultivation;
one should not emanate what is unstable. Thus, that which is being cultivated should not be emanated [if unstable], but should be emanated by means of excellent clouds.
When the emanation of the vajras and so forth has been made stable, one should also emanate clouds of Buddhas with splendors equal to the flames of a Buddha,
appearing in colors such as white and the rest.
He states the method for its cultivation:
"One who eats alms-food should not mutter.

This means that a yogin who practices the conduct of the utterly peaceful and free from conceptual proliferation, while receiving alms for the sake of begging, should not engage in idle chatter with persistent effort, saying, "Give me alms-food."
"And one should not be intent on alms" means that one should not be attached to food; rather, one should be content with just as much as is necessary for the maintenance of the body,
or else—
Alms are obtained there through such division; therefore, one should not recite [mantras] there,
or rather,
why should one ever be fond of division?
To that end, he says:
"And one should not be intent on begging" (na ca bhaikṣarato bhavet); this is the meaning:
[not even] once, twice, or three times.
While conceptualizing, when one perceives the maṇḍala circle very clearly, then the mind should remain fixed upon that alone;
and it has been said in another place:
"By whatever state the minds of men are joined..."
Through that, one attains identity with it, just as a gem assumes the form of everything around it; for this very reason, it is said that "one should recite the mantra as an inseparable limb.
By means of this, through the stability of the mind, the practitioner—being devoid of all external conceptual constructions—directly realizes the maṇḍala circle as being like an illusion.
And it is said in another tantra:
"Just as the moon in the midst of water is neither real nor unreal, so too that body,
by its very nature, is pure within the circle of the mandalas."
By this, the second samādhi named Maṇḍalarājāgra is [concluded].
Now, in order to explain the two-fold division of the vocal recitation (*vāgjāpa*) of the three syllables, he says: "One should emanate the vajra by uttering... and so forth;
having uttered [the syllables], he speaks of the two-fold division of the vocal recitation.
"Having recited, one should emanate the vajra," and so forth.

Having recited by means of the door of speech, and having obtained the three-syllabled vajra from the *nāda* of the Samādhisattva, one should emanate it externally; then, by means of the entering breath, one should reabsorb it into that very same place—this is the "lump-recitation" (*piṇḍajāpa*).
This is the mantra-recitation belonging even to all the Buddhas, that is, the five Tathāgatas. Therefore, this indeed is the mantra-recitation.

By this, the recitation (*japa*) performed through the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*)—which is explained by dividing it into two ways—is also elucidated. One should cause [the mind] to enter into suchness (*tathatā*); thus, that which is the attainment of mind-only (*cittamātratā*) by means of the subtle yoga as established is precisely its object of focus (*ālambana*), namely suchness.
In this way, the Great Vajradhara is of the nature of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).

Having seen that his four beloved consorts, Locanā and the others, whose natures consist of loving-kindness and so forth, were suffering in mind due to separation from him and were longing for a sight of him, he spoke with compassion so that they might see him,
in the four verses beginning with "The four goddesses situated in the mandala," and so on.

With *ṣāḍava* and other notes, accompanied by sweet sounds faltering with *kākalī*, they awaken and rouse him by means of hymns, as if visualizing him standing right before them, saying "You. Because he has attained mastery over the mind (*vajracitta*), he has attained the sovereignty over the single Dharma of the three realms; thus he is the Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśvara*). Since he consists of the very nature of the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), he is the *sattvabhūta*. He is "delightful to the mind" (*ratimanojña*) because his play (*rati*) generates joy.

The Great Purpose is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*); those who desire—that is, bring about—that [bliss] are "those who desire the great purpose" (*mahārthakāmāḥ*). By means of such methods of delight that are pleasing to the mind—such as embracing and so forth—and by those who desire the great purpose, do not abandon me (*mā kā māhi*); rather, take pleasure in me. Because you are the cause for the arising of all sentient beings, you are the "progenitor" (*janaka*) of beings; because you bring about the fundamental happiness of beings, you are the "supreme kinsman of beings" (*satvamahāgrabandhu*). O Protector, O Lord, if you so desire, [then remain] within me, my very life. "You are the Vajra-body," and so forth.
Because your body is indestructible, you possess a vajra-body;
because you issue commands beloved by many sentient beings, you are the "Command-Wheel" (*ājñācakra*). You act for the benefit of many sentient beings because you turn the wheel of command.
You are the one who perceives the welfare of the ultimate goal of awakening and the ultimate truth of the Buddhas' purpose.

The Buddhas are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); their object is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), while awakening (*bodhi*) is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). The form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) born from the union of these two is the ultimate reality. Because it is revealed to sentient beings with the intention of their welfare, it is the "perceiver of welfare. Through the disease of passion in the form of its purification, [the Buddha] is the one who, by means of the pledge of passion (*rāgasamayā*)—whose nature is the conduct of passion—enjoys Māmakī. You are "Vajra Speech" (*vajravāc*) because you have attained mastery over speech. You are the one who has compassion for the welfare of the entire realm of sentient beings, being characterized by supreme mercy.

For this very reason, he is always and at all times correctly engaged in acting for the benefit of sentient beings through the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). He is Samantabhadra because he brings about universal welfare and auspiciousness for the entire realm of sentient beings (*satvadhātu*) by means of the practice of supreme delight (*suratacaryā*). The other [name] is analyzed as follows: he addresses him by way of Amoghasiddhi, saying, "O Vajrakāya.

Because the deities of the maṇḍala are emitted from the union of the vajra and the lotus, and because he purifies the realm of sentient beings who are characterized by hatred and so forth, he is Vajrakāma.

Because he is the sovereign of the Karma family, he is the foremost of the Samayas; because he bestows liberation upon beings whose conduct is dominated by passion through the means of purifying that passion, he is of great benefit;
and because he is the preeminent ornament among those born of the Śākya lineage, he is the Ornament of the Lineage of the Perfectly Awakened Ones (Sambuddhavaṃśatilaka).

Alternatively, because you fulfill the welfare of the entire world through the nature of the knowledge of performing what is to be done, you are the ornament of the lineage of the Perfectly Awakened Ones.

Although you are devoid of the perception of the distinction between self and other in reality, you are compassionate toward sentient beings due to your mercy; thus, being one who possesses equal compassion and is a treasure-house of virtues, a source of many jewels—desire me, who am distinguished by such qualities, and take me as your consort.
Because she praises herself, saying, "I am the one who generates the supreme gnosis that illuminates passion, dispassion, and intermediate passion," [the meaning is:
"O Protector, if you wish to live, give me life!"—the intention being:
"Live by means of the purification of passion, hatred, and delusion through the bestowal of the life and youth of Vajrasattva. Thus, and so forth.

Thus, being exhorted by the goddesses whose nature consists of the four Brahma-vihāras through the proclamation of his truly existing qualities, the Lord, the Protector— who had arisen from the yoga of emptiness as if awakened from sleep by the power of the continuity of his former vows— is immediately thereafter praised by the Tathāgatas, Vairocana and the others, who are themselves of the nature of Akṣobhya and so forth, with the verses to be recited beginning with "Akṣobhya... and so on.

"O Akṣobhyavajra"—this is an address to one whose adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) is immovable and unshakable by the arrays of all afflictions (*kleśa*). This [epithet] should also be understood in such passages as "the great wise one, the gnosis of the body-maṇḍala," and so forth;
he is "of great gnosis" (*mahājñāna*) because his nature consists of the four voids (*caturśūnya*).
The "Vajras" are Akṣobhya and the others; he who holds them is the Vajradhātu.
Because of his thorough knowledge of the distinction between the two truths, he is the Great Wise One (*mahābuddha*).
He is the "Three Mandalas," being the nature of the Body Mandala, the Emanation Mandala, and the Ultimate Mandala.
Because he is preeminent among the vajras of body and so forth, he is "the foremost of the three vajras" (*trivajrāgra*).
They praised him through the gateway of Akṣobhya, saying: "Reveal to us the reality of the equality of the secret speech. Regarding "Vairocana" and so forth:
he is Vairocana because he shines by means of the fire of clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
Therefore, he is the Great Pure One (*mahāśuddha*).
Because the Tathāgatas are vajras, and because he is the sixth by virtue of their state of purity, he is Vajraśānta. Since his nature is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), he is Mahārati.

"Teach"—that is, reveal—the phenomena (*dharmas*) which are luminous by nature (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*). He addresses him as "Vajra. [The passage] beginning with "O King of Jewels" (*ratnarāja*) and so forth...
Because he bestows knowledge that is never fruitless, he is Amoghavajra (Infallible Vajra).

He is the Perfectly Awakened One (*sambuddha*) who is honored by those belonging to the Amogha family; thus, as Amoghavajra-sambuddha, he fulfills all hopes because he accomplishes the intentions of practitioners through rites such as pacification (*śānti*).
