Being pure, his intrinsic nature is luminous (*prabhāsvara*); because he originates from that, he is "born from the pure intrinsic nature" (*śuddhasvabhāvasambhūta*).

"O Vajrasattva who has become thus, homage to you"—this is the conclusion of the hymn of praise. Having praised himself by means of the Buddhas, such as Vairocana and others, acting as the instruments; having delighted the circle of goddesses through the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); having revealed the secret [teachings] such as protection and so forth; and having performed the recitation of the two kinds of mantras as taught according to the distinctions of the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and so on; one should cause the external circle to enter into one's own body-circle by way of "transcending the aggregate of form" and so forth, and then arise everywhere with the nature of great bliss, free from attachment.
The third samādhi, the foremost king of activities, is concluded. Now, he speaks regarding the training for the purpose of dwelling:
"Thus, one who performs the four yogas," and so forth.
The meaning is that a yogin endowed with the four yogas in the manner described above, being possessed of the three samādhis, should perform his dwelling in that way and not otherwise.
"Containing the syllable *hūṃ*":

having summoned all sentient beings here by means of the light rays of the Samādhisattva and caused them to enter right there, one should again emanate them from that [state] in the form of Vajrasattva; then, with that very form, one should dwell with a mind focused on that [deity].
And it has been said by the Noble Ones:

"This is a gabled pavilion, not the triple world; these are not living beings, but Jinas; he here is the Lord of the Wheel, not a human; there are no sense objects, no sense faculties, nor earth and the other elements; and these deities of the mandala are not composed of form and so forth by way of their true nature. As you contemplate the entire universe as the wheel of the mandala, why does your mind wander? When the practitioner of the mantra-mandala wheel becomes emaciated in body, he speaks the words beginning with "only a span" (*vitastimātram*) and so forth, demonstrating the nourishment of the body through another form of meditative concentration.
One should visualize the conceptualization of a moon disc produced from the transformation of the syllable *dhava* in the sky above one’s head.

Then, having meditated on the syllable *oṃ* as entering [the body] and situated in the center of that moon disc, the descent of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) should be performed. Because they do not die by means of these, they are the "five nectars," which are the five Tathāgatas; their descent should be performed as a consecration (*abhiṣeka*) from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet, by way of the nature of five rays of light.

By means of this aforementioned vajra-yoga which has the Tathāgata as its object, one becomes radiant and possessed of a beautiful body; one is born [thus] in an instant, and before long, one obtains and attains the excellence of the body and so forth—this is the benefit (*anuśaṃsā*). Alternatively, he speaks of the method of internal nourishment (*āpyāyana*).
Having placed the tongue against the palate, one should contemplate the tip of the nose;
through the touch of the face of the subtle vajra,
the mind becomes concentrated.
"Thus, through practice, the yogi... and so forth is the statement of the summary (*uddeśapada*).
"By means of the syllable *hūṃ*," and so forth, is the statement of its detailed explanation (*nirdeśapada*).
"By means of the syllable *hūṃ*, etc.

The meaning of this is as follows: First, one should visualize a greenish-black wind mandala produced from two *hūṃ* seeds, shaped like a bow, marked with two vajras, and blazing. Above that, one should visualize a triangular fire mandala of red color, produced from two *hūṃ* seeds, marked with two vajras. Above that, one sees a lotus vessel transformed from the syllable *āḥ*, white on the outside and red on the inside, and empowered by the syllable *āḥ*. In the center of that [vessel] is the food, consisting of various types of eatables and the like.

*Bum ām jrīm kham hūṃ*. Thus, the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*) and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), such as cow dung and so forth, are transformed from these seed-syllables; they consist of the nature of the five gnoses and are marked with the syllable *oṃ*. Within that space, one should stir them with a white vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*. By means of this syllable *hūṃ*, purification occurs through the union of the vajra and lotus vessels, whereby the vajra becomes of one flavor (*samarasībhūta*) right there.
Awakening by means of the syllable *ĀḤ*, and blazing forth by means of the syllable *Oṃ* which shines like the sun of gnosis—by these, the nectar of the commitment (*samaya*) is produced.

Abiding therein, one brings forth the nectar of the gnosis of the Tathāgatas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions by means of the streams of radiating light from the three syllables; having cast this into the nectar of the commitment, it is empowered by the three syllables seven times. This is the purification of the food offering.
From "A conch at the throat" up to "the purification of the throat," this is clear from the very beginning with respect to the practice of Akṣobhya. Regarding "Meghanāda" and so forth:
Meghanāda;
the syllable *hūṃ* in the heart.
Having meditated on the three-pointed fire, one should then emanate it and offer food into it; this is the internal *homa*.

Thus, the yogin of Vairocana and the others, having produced the signs such as the wheel—which have arisen from their respective seed-syllables placed upon a conch and a lotus within the mouth and are empowered by syllables such as Oṃ—should, according to the distinctions of the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth, offer food into the three-pointed fire of the Samādhisattva appropriate to each, according to the oral tradition.

The passage beginning with "vāyavyam" and ending with "sarvopadravanāśanam" is easy to understand. Within this very section, there is the phrase "by means of the yoga of *sampuṭīkaraṇa*. Its explanation is: because of the restraint (*yantraṇāt*) of the upward and downward winds.
The commentary on "Śrīvajramālā," etc., is also even more explicit.
Thus ends the *Yogimanoharā* commentary on the *Piṇḍīkrama*.

Now, in order to demonstrate the explanation of the *vajrajāpa* within the *Piṇḍīkrama*, having already established the isolation of the body (*kāyaviveka*), he says, beginning with "consisting of the essence of all sentient beings," etc., regarding the Lord who has become a protector:
of what nature is he?

Having bowed down— that is, having paid homage— to the Glorious One who consists of great bliss, who is endowed with the glory of both, and who is the *cittavajra* (mind-vajra) associated with wind and consciousness, which is the self (*ātman*) of all sentient beings; for "all sentient beings" means all those living creatures (*prāṇin*) dwelling in every world, and their "self" is that very *cittavajra*.
I shall explain the sequence of vajra-recitation; that is, I will describe it. From what source? In accordance with the Yoga Tantra.
[Yoga Tantra]
The *Śrī-samāja* and other tantras;
following them and through the realization of their meaning,
he says [the following] in order to demonstrate the sequence for crossing over by means of vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*).
"Of those established in the stage of generation," and so forth;
that is, of those established in the stage of generation who have realized the *piṇḍīkrama* (the condensed stage),
and who desire the form of the *niṣpannakrama* (the completion stage) in the state of union (*yuganaddha*).
This vajra-recitation is the means— the cause— for those yogins who desire and seek to attain the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*);
and it has been fashioned and demonstrated by the Perfectly Awakened Ones (*samyaksambuddha*), just like a staircase.
"Being the life-force," and so forth;
"called wind" (*vāyvākhyaḥ*): that whose name or designation (*ākhyā*) is "wind" (*vāyu*) is "called wind."
He is the life-force and the very essence of living beings and the worlds;
because he performs all actions,
such as contracting and extending [the limbs], he is called the "performer of all actions" (*sarvakarmakṛt*).
"Consciousness is the vehicle," meaning it serves as the mount for consciousness, like a rider on a horse.
Now, one might ask: "In that case, how can wind and consciousness possess appearance (*sābhāsatva*)?

Since the wind element is formless and consciousness is also formless, the establishment of their respective objects by each of these through its own inherent nature is not possible. This is the question.
To this, the following reply is given:
Because the wind and consciousness become unified and thus apprehend objects, it is said to possess an appearance (*sābhāsa*).
And so it was stated in the *Anuttarasandhi*:
"When joined with the appearance, the wind has become a vehicle," and so forth in detail.
That very [wind], called *vāyu*, consists of fivefold nature and becomes five types.
How so? *Prāṇa* is in the heart, *apāna* in the anus, and *samāna* is situated throughout the body.
According to the principle that *udāna* is located in the region of the throat while *vyāna* pervades the entire body,
that very [prāṇa] further becomes fivefold and then tenfold,
by virtue of its presence in the eyes and other [senses], such as the nāgas, together with their respective appearances (*sābhāsa*).
And so it is said in the *Anuttarasandhi*:
"When joined with the appearance (*ābhāsa*), the wind becomes the vehicle," and so forth in detail. That very same [wind], called "wind," consists of fivefold nature and becomes five types.
How?
According to the principle that "prāṇa is in the heart, apāna is in the anus, samāna is situated in the navel,

udāna is in the region of the throat, and vyāna pervades the entire body," that very [wind] further becomes fivefold, and then tenfold, together with nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya, which reside in the eyes and other [senses].
"By means of the sequence of the wind element," and so forth, up to "through the purity of the supreme light"—having thus analyzed the meaning of the four stages, [it is said]:
"by means of the sequence of the wind element. Without the reality of mantra (*mantratattva*), one would not enter; rather, one enters by means of the three-syllable mantras.
The thorough knowledge of these [three] by way of their intrinsic nature as entering, abiding, and emerging is the "contemplation of mantra" (*mantranidhyapti*).
Having attained—that is, having reached—that, one becomes well-trained in vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*). What is the meaning of "abiding in vajra-recitation"?
The mantra practitioner, the yogin established in the samādhi of the direct realization of vajra-recitation, should attain and obtain the profound contemplation of the mind (*cittanidhyapti*).
How so? Because speech and mind abide in a state of oneness by way of the relationship between the support and the supported.
Regarding the thorough knowledge of reality as it is through the second stage of mental absorption,
some here declare that in vajra-recitation, vocal isolation alone is supreme.
The claim that "mental isolation" (*cittaviveka*) occurs through the unsurpassed bond (*anuttarasandhi*) is not tenable;
for, according to the explanation of the venerable master Candrakīrti, it is said that the mere contemplation of the mind (*cittanidhyaptimātra*) constitutes the second stage,
and this very point is stated here in the context of the stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*).

"One who has attained the isolation (*viveka*) of body, speech, and mind" means that, therefore, by the very second stage, there is the contemplation (*nidhyapti*) of speech and mind as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), and thus the two types of knowledge are unreal (*alīka*). "Abiding in the illusion-like samādhi" refers to the five [aspects] according to the division of the *Kṛtaprabheda*: the unreality of the body in the *Piṇḍīkrama*, and the unreality of speech and mind in the *Vajrajāpa*—each separately.
The "union of the three" (*trisamyoga*) refers to that in which there is a conjunction—that is, a unification—of these three knowledges;

it is the form of the deity, characterized by self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) and resembling an illusion, which is inseparable from the three vajras. The "illusion-like meditative absorption" (*māyopama-samādhi*) is that state, and the yogin established therein is absorbed in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

For, according to the principle that "the clear light is indeed attained through the sequence of self-consecration," the method of investigation consisting in the meditative realization of body, speech, and mind—
which has the nature of conventional truth— is not perceived once it has been attained.

Because it leads all beings to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), this reveals the sequence of manifest enlightenment (*abhisambodhikrama*). "Arising from the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭeḥ*) means arising from that [limit] by way of its causal sign;
it is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*).
One should attain—that is, obtain—knowledge free from duality;
for it has been said by the Noble One:
"Just as a fish quickly leaps out from clear river water..."

Likewise, according to the principle that "the net of illusion (māyājāla) arises from the luminous and pure," the yogi established in the samādhi of union (yuganaddha)— that is, established in the samādhi of perfect enlightenment— learns nothing further and becomes one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
By this very sequence, he who is called the yoga of the completed stage (*niṣpannakrama*) becomes that Great Vajradhara;
furthermore,
all [attributes] such as "endowed with the excellence of all aspects" (*sarvākāravaropeta*) are indeed qualifications of the Great Vajradhara alone.
"This reality is established," and so forth—

this which has been stated and explained is that reality which is well-sealed in the *tantra* and concealed by *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language). It should be understood from the mouth of the Guru (*guruvaktrataḥ*), following and in accordance with the *Vyākhyātantra*, the *Vajramālā*, and other such works, [obtained] from the presence of the Guru.
Regarding the word *tatra*: in that fivefold wind;

"first of all" (*prathamataram*) means that this is the first [practice] after the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*). This Vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*), beginning with self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth, is the most excellent among these two. This Vajra-recitation is introduced—that is, explained—by being brought down from the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*) in the chapter concerning the nature of the winds (*vāyutattva*).
The explanation, detailed exposition, and commentary of this very [work] will be the text to be spoken from the *Mūlatantra*,
the *Śrīsamāja-tantra*.

"One should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose," and so forth. "At the tip of the nose" means in the upper nostril. One should contemplate—that is, observe—a mustard seed, which refers to the subtle wind. How is it that the word "mustard seed" (*sarṣapa*) denotes the element of wind? To this he replies:

because it "moves" (*salati*) or "goes" (*gacchati*), according to the rule for the *uṇādi* suffix *apaṣ* added to the root *sṛ*; thus, the mustard seed is the wind, by virtue of the common property of subtlety.

Within a mustard seed, within the subtle element of the mustard seed, one should meditate upon the three syllables— which constitute the support and the supported— along with the wind, as entering, abiding, and emerging as one;
this is the state of gnosis (*jñānapada*).
The three knowledges are its *pada*, which is a synonym for its foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) or support (*āśraya*).

It is "delightful" (*ramya*), meaning beautiful, because it possesses the nature of the dark-blue [mandala] and so forth, together with the mandalas of wind and the other elements; it is "secret" (*rahasya*), meaning well-guarded.
For the practitioners of the Vajrajāpa yoga alone,
it is conceptualized through gnosis by means of entry, abiding, and exit.
In the wind, the conceptualized five-colored [mantra] consisting of three syllables of the nature of gnosis, and so forth—
that very same subtle wind-element endowed with colors such as white and the rest.
The great jewel, like a great jewel, is priceless;
it is the size of a mustard seed, as subtle as the element of air within a mustard seed, and is clearly [visualized] at the tip of the nose according to the previous explanation.
One should bring [the deity] forth with effort— that is, with great exertion— either through yoga by way of the nature of the four mandalas beginning with wind,
or instantaneously by way of the mental support of the three faces, six arms, and so forth.
He states the explanation of this term as "sandhyābhāṣā" (intentional language) at all times,
in the *Caturdevīparipṛcchāvyākhyātantra*.
"Regarding 'tad devi' and so forth:
'devi' is an address to the Goddess;
I shall fully explain—that is, I shall relate—the words of the Blessed One."
The Vajra-recitation is more essential than even the essence, the Piṇḍīkrama; it is supreme.
The supreme secret,
well-guarded by all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, which is characterized by the vajra-recitation.
That [wind] remains conjoined with consciousness within the self of all things, or within the selves of all sentient beings of the three realms;
it consists of the five wisdoms, and so forth, because its intrinsic nature is that of the five Tathāgatas.

The reality consisting of the five cognitions, such as the mirror-like wisdom and so forth, has the nature of wind and is the size of a mustard seed; this is clear from the previous explanation. The deity resides in the center of that wind.

Abiding by way of the nature of the three syllables is due to the non-difference between the mantra and the deity through identity (*tādātmya*). It is "unmanifest" because it is difficult to grasp and because it has a subtle form; yet it "possesses a manifest form" because it is followed by actions such as contraction, expansion, and movement.
Alternatively:

The *Samājottara* also elucidates this very same point, stating "consisting of the five cognitions" and so forth, [explaining that] the unmanifest [wind] becomes manifest in the form of earth and the other elements, while [the wind itself] remains manifest in the form of air.

When this breath, which is situated above and has the nature of the five cognitions such as the mirror-like [wisdom], moves downward—that very [breath] having the nature of the five elements and consisting of earth and so forth—through the union of the two organs and the meditative absorption of internal wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), it is impelled by joy. Having melted all the limbs with the fire of great passion (*mahārāga*), it issues forth from the opening of the natural *vajra* in the form of a mass, in the form of a drop of *bodhicitta*, and falls upon the tip of the lotus nose.
This [seed-syllable] has been designated by the Tathāgatas with the word "mustard seed" for those who contemplate the stages of the arising of existence;
and it is said in the Tantra:
"The nectar is called semen (*śukra*); from that, the three worlds are produced. [It is] "five-colored," and so forth.

That very upward-moving breath, which consists of the five Tathāgatas and is therefore the Great Jewel (*mahāratna*), is that by which the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—life itself—is extended (*āyāmyate*) or lengthened (*vistāryate*); thus it is known as *prāṇāyāma-vāyu*.

Having meditated upon that very [breath] as one's own mantra—the syllable *HŪṂ*—in the heart, because it is recited day and night through its nature of entering [the body] and so forth; and having placed the mind within the drop (*bindu*)—that is, the sound produced from the syllable *HŪṂ*, known as the Unstruck (*anāhata*), in the form of a subtle drop—one should contemplate it, making the mind enter into that state. This is the intended meaning.
In this context, how is the mind designated by the word "vital breath" (*prāṇa*)?
For "vital breath," "mind," and "life-force" (*jīvita*) are synonyms.

Since *prāṇa* is the mind (*citta*), as stated in the *Matitantra*, it is precisely for this reason that *prāṇāyāma* is said to be a limb within the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*). Regarding the application and explanation of the five-limbed yoga beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) in the *Vajrajāpakrama* and the other four stages, no detailed exposition has been provided here for fear of excessive length. If there is an intention to apply [the method] to those [stages], then a complete explanation is given in the commentary on the Tantra composed by Ācārya Candrakīrti; having understood that, the application should be made by practitioners. He provides a specific instruction regarding that as well:
In the explanatory tantra named *Vajramālā*,
[the section] beginning with "at the tip of the nose" and ending with "the internal time is taught" [is stated].

This explanation of the previously stated instruction is now explained by means of a further detailed exposition (*pratinirdeśa*). "A mustard seed at the tip of the nose" refers to the conceptualization of the wind of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the nature of the five Buddhas. Those very five rays, abiding within the wind of breath-control, become the breath-control itself; having emerged from the aperture of breath-control at the upper tip of the nose, they issue forth through the sequence of arising and so forth, distinguished as left, right, and so on—thus there would be four ways. That [breath] itself becomes fourfold. By this, the internal time is remembered and understood. One should contemplate the mustard seed at the tip of the nose. One explanation has already been stated for the preceding verse of the instruction; the second explanation is to be understood by the practitioner (*bhāvaka*) by taking it from that [context].
Regarding this, he said: "One should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose"—this is the meaning of this vajra-word;
by this, both the reality of wind and the reality of mantra are explained.

"In the mustard seed, together with the moving and the unmoving" means that within the mustard seed—the subtle wind-element—one should contemplate and understand the threefold consciousness (*vijñānatraya*), which consists of the support and the supported, and whose nature is awakening. One should meditate upon this reality (*tattva*) as follows: "The delightful state of knowledge, the secret fashioned by knowledge.
This "state of knowledge" is the body of wind-consciousness; this very state is the delightful culmination.

It is not an object for those yogins who conceptualize (*kalpita-yogin*), because its intrinsic nature is the luminous gnosis (*prabhāsvara-jñāna*). By the phrase "conceptualized by gnosis," the reality of the deity (*devatā-tattva*) is expressed. It is not known from which [source] the five rays—which have been mentioned immediately above as having the nature of the five gnoses—come and circulate through the upper nostril; for that purpose, he says: "In the throat," and so forth. This is easy to understand. However, here the arrangement of the flow of the winds through the four mandalas of the throat and so on is shown with reference to the body, not according to the sequence of their movement; the sequence of movement is indeed of a different kind.
And it has been stated by the venerable master Candrakīrti in his *Tantraṭīkā*: "He explains that interpretation thus:
'In the heart is the water-maṇḍala; in the throat is the fire-maṇḍala;
in the secret place is the earth-maṇḍala.'"

At the navel is the wind-maṇḍala; these, beginning with the water-maṇḍala, are endowed with white and other rays and reside within all bodies. Upon their arising, one should describe their coming and going through the process of inhalation and exhalation, relying on the distinctions in the sequence of pacifying rites (*śāntika*) and so forth. By means of the successive rotation of the four maṇḍalas, one should dwell and move according to the sequence, without transgressing the proper order, for half a watch (*yāma*) of time. Now, the regulation of the deities according to the different colors of the flow of the maṇḍalas is clear from the very beginning, starting with "from the right" and so forth.
"Unapproachable for immature yogins"— this [phrase] is very easy to understand;
thus,

having established the reality of the winds (*vāyutatva*) through the sequence of brief statement and detailed exposition, the reality of mantra (*mantratatva*) is now explained by this same sequence.
In that regard, first of all, the brief exposition of the fourfold reality of mantra is set forth:
"The secret of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas" is the form of the deity known as *upalambha*, because it arises from these three syllables: Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ.
"This is called the supreme secret, the impelling of the heart of all mantras.

Because of his devotion to the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) of that very mantra, he proclaimed the *Mantrasamuccaya*— the ultimate bodhicitta which is devoid of intrinsic nature— from his own vajras of body, speech, and mind, by means of verbal expression and linguistic analysis.

"From the utterance" means from the pronunciation of "oṃ āḥ hūṃ. Regarding the phrase "following the meaning" and so forth: the meaning of the syllables *oṃ* and the others is "entry" and so on; the recitation (*jāpa*) performed by following—that is, in accordance with—that meaning is what is intended.

By that reason—by means of that which is essence-less (*niḥsvabhāva*), unstruck (*anāhata*), beautiful, and of a continuously vibrating nature—there occurs the investigation, discernment, and thorough knowledge of the Buddhas of the three times, that is, the Tathāgatas existing in the three periods; it is the realization of all Tathāgatas in the form of the Unstruck (*anāhata*).
By this, the symbolic (*sāṃketika*) mantra-reality is shown;
for among the four kinds of mantras, the symbolic mantra is declared to be the primary one.

How so? Because of the introduction to the isolation of speech (*vāk-viveka*). And it has been stated in the *Sūtaka* that the culmination of the isolation of speech is the thorough knowledge of the *vajrajāpa* alone.
The *vajra* is the wind; its recitation (*jāpa*) is as follows:
because it is a natural recitation (*prakṛtijāpa*), that recitation which is not heard by others is called *vajrajāpa*.
It is described [in the text] beginning with "one who eats alms-food" (*bhikṣāśin*).
One who has the habit of eating alms-food should not recite [the mantra], nor should he look about.
"Eating alms-food" is used as an illustration; therefore, one should not recite while engaged in other modes of wretched livelihood such as wandering for alms and so forth.
Nor should one be devoted to begging. "Begging" (bhaikṣa) is an illustration for material gain (āmiṣa).

One should not be intent on alms-seeking nor addicted to food; being content with just as much as is necessary for the maintenance of the body, one must engage in a practice that is utterly free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
To the question of what a yogin established in such a practice should do, [the text] says: "He should recite," and so forth.

"One should recite the three-syllable mantra with its limbs undivided"—this refers to the yoga of the indivisible deity, which effects the enjoyment of all desires; thus the practitioner should recite.

Alternatively, the wind exits in the very form of the mantra and not separately; one should not form a conceptual distinction such as "this is the wind" and "this is the mantra. For this very reason, it says: "one should recite the mantra with its limbs undivided."

He states the detailed explanation corresponding to the summary heading within the mantra explained in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇa*: "Then he replied," and so forth; "he replied" means that the illustrious Vajrapāṇi makes a request.
The all-pervading Mahāvairocana is Vajrasattva of manifold forms; this is the mind.
The mind has the world as its intrinsic nature because it arises from the birth of all sentient beings,
due to the production of all sentient beings. "It is born," and so forth.
The mind being thus,
although it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is "born"— that is, first arisen— due to dependence,
namely through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Just like a reflection in a mirror, by this causal process it becomes what is called "existence" (*bhava*).

Having made such a mind one's own experience through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), one should correctly bring the *bodhicitta*—which has the nature of *bodhicitta* and is equal to space, resembling the sky—to its fulfillment. And in order to accomplish the welfare of the world, one should teach that [mind] to superior persons; thus I shall explain it in detail. This King of Four Mantras was taught by the Blessed One himself according to the reality of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpārthatattva*) from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*). It is extremely easy to understand, as it is the reality of non-conceptual meaning.
He says that he now points out what was previously indicated:
"that which is called conventional, consisting of verbal expression and perception, is the ultimate"—
this is a further explanation of that very same point.

"Verbal expression is indeed the common [element]," and so forth; this is the detailed explanation. "Common" refers to the utterance of the subsequent words, which will be specifically pointed out immediately after the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*).
Having brought that [point] here, a clearer explanation should be understood by the wise.
Now he states the extraction of the recitation of the uttered words,
beginning with "one and so forth," [referring to] "by means of the sixteen vowels beginning with 'a'."
One group is ña-ña-ṇa-na-ma;
the second, excluding na-ña-ṇa-na-ma, consists of the consonants beginning with ka, arranged in groups of four syllables each.

The seven groups are to be taken; among these nine groups, whichever is the first letter is to be taken. It is "one" because there is no other of its own kind [preceding it]. And it is "first" (*ādi*); thus, the vowel *a*, which is the first of the vowels beginning with *e*.
Because it is recited at the beginning; one should understand that this, being the first of the groups (varga), has a connection with what follows— how so?

Because they are included within that [group]. Just as the *kṛta* age is called "the *kṛta* among the ages," the meaning is that it is situated in the middle of the ages. The word *tu* is for the purpose of completing the meter.
In the phrase "by ten" (*daśabhiḥ*) and so forth, the word "ten" (*daśa*) denotes groups of ten.
In this context, the forty-nine phonemes from *a* to *ha* are to be taken; by grouping them into four sets of ten, they become forty.

He extracts [the letter *ha*], which consists of nine syllables. One should understand that the letter *ha* is that which is not bound, or not connected, by these ten—meaning, by the ten groups (*daśavarga*). "He knows it" is easy to understand.

Now, regarding the phrase "the nine in the middle" (*navamadhya*), in order to dispel the doubt as to whether the word "nine" (*nava*) refers to the vowels beginning with *a* that have been grouped together, or to some other [set], he says "vowels" (*svara*) and so forth, clarifying that the "vowels" are those beginning with *a*.
The consonants are ña, ña, ṇa, na, ma;
the remaining ones are understood, the letter ca being used for emphasis.
Therefore, they should be understood as following the number nine;
the meaning is that they follow the number expressed by the word "nine" and are thus comprised within the word "nine.
Are these two—the letter *a* and the letter *ha*—mere [phonemes]?
[The question arises: "Are they connected with another phoneme? To this he says, "unbound," and so forth;
that is, the phonemes beginning with *ka* are unbound, meaning they are not joined with the phoneme *a*.
"From the cause of mutual conjunction," "up to the end of the elements," and so forth; the "elements" (bhūta) refer to the five great elements (pañcamahābhūta).

Here, the word *bhūta* in the compound *bhūtānte* is like the designation "cloth" applied to the edge of a cloth. Therefore, the short *u* in *bhūta-* is [the first member], and this word *anta* denotes that which is proximate to what has come into being (*bhūta*). Because it is the subject under discussion, it is understood as "of the *bhūta*";
for words function according to the speaker's intention and not by way of an inherent restrictive rule.
The long *ū* is included by the word "ending," but the *ī* is not;
and since it is both "existent" (*bhūta*) and "at the end" (*anta*), it is called "existent-ending" (*bhūtānta*).
That which is joined with this [long *ū*]—namely, the pair of phonemes mentioned immediately above—is [to be understood as occurring] "subsequently" (*parataḥ*); this is the ellipsis.
Regarding the term "kalādi" and so forth: it is both *kalā* (a digit/part) and *ādi* (the first), hence *kalādi*.
*Kalā* refers to the sixteen digits; those which are purified by them are the sixteen vowels. Among these, the syllable that constitutes their beginning is the letter *a*.
The meaning is that he does not merely abide in the sixteenth, such as the *kalā*, but is the fulfiller of the sixteen; he is established beyond this sixteenth as the syllable *Āḥ*.

Regarding the phrase "conjoined with five fives," by the word "one five" (*ekapañca*), one should take the fifth group after having enumerated the five groups by means of the five-syllabled [sequence].
The fifth of that fifth group is the letter *ma*;
it is conjoined with, that is, closely connected to, that [letter].

Alternatively, by the term "the other five," the letter *m* is the fifth of the groups [of consonants] beginning with *ña*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma*; that which is joined with it is "joined with the four. As for "three and three and three," the term "three" is used as a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*).
"Four and three" means four and three; by them, the "three places" are enjoined—that is, bound—according to their respective application. The three are the syllables A, U, and Ma.
In the middle, there are two *a*s, the *visarga*, and the *ma*;
thus there are four syllables. Alternatively, there are three: the final *ha*, the *ū*, and the *ma*.
(Alternatively:
there are two *a*-sounds and the letter *ha*;
these are the three phonemes.
Among these, the four phonemes should be applied.
Which are they? They are the phonemes *u*, *a*, *ū*, and *m*. But surely, since two instances of the phoneme *m* are produced here, how can it be designated by a single [term]?
Because of the homogeneity of the letter *m*.
Regarding "with an anusvāra":
in the first and remaining positions, there is an anusvāra for the letter *m*; in the second position, when a long vowel follows, there is a long vowel for the letter *a* [of the prefix].
Like the elision resulting from the combination of *guṇa* qualities:
there is a *guṇa* substitution of the vowel *a* with *u*, resulting in *o*;
this is the first [case], while the conjunction of *anusvāra* with the first and third [consonants] is the second.
In the second [case], there is also elision of the *m* following the *visarga* when combined with the letter *u*.

Alternatively, regarding the rule "like the elision of *guṇa* and *saṃyoga*," how is there elision of the *u* by means of that elision? In the rule "for *u*-vowels, *o*," the *u* becomes *o*, and the subsequent [element] is elided.
There is the elision of the letter *u*.
Demonstrating that the letter *a* is the foremost among its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), he says "the short," and so forth.
The short *a* is [the primary element] because it functions as the cause for the operation of the entire sentence.
Without that [articulation], it is impossible to utter anything at all—
neither many nor one. Since it occurs in respect to multiple phonemes, how could it be one with respect to each individual one?
Because it belongs to the genus consisting of the mere letter *a*, it is not manifold; this is what is meant by the words "those which are the phonemes" (*ye varṇāḥ*), and so forth.
Immediately after the vowel *ā*, the consonant *k* is pronounced; because it is pronounced for the sake of the meaning, there is a state of being turned away from the back [of the preceding sound].
Or else:
Because both [the vowels and consonants] are pronounced in sequence according to the rule *a-ā-ka-kha-*, [the genders are assigned as follows]:
excluding *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*, all vowels (*ālaḥ*) are designated as feminine (*strī*). "Feminine, masculine, and neuter" [is the classification].

Excluding *ña*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *ma*, and *ma*, the designation "male" (*puruṣa*) applies to the vowels [excluding *a*]. That which is excluded from the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*) is the neuter (*napuṃsaka*).

Regarding the phrase "and those": those aforementioned [vowels] are the middle ones by virtue of their meaning; the vowel *āḥ* is the middle one. These three syllables are situated at the beginning, middle, and end according to the order of recitation.
Having understood this through the intellect, one should apply oneself and practice it. He now provides a detailed explanation of what was previously indicated:

"This utterance of mantra arises from a nature that is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). From that, form is transformed, which brings about the perception of the deity; it is conventional, established in the three principles (*tritattva*), and characterized by natural recitation."

Regarding the passage beginning with "the enumeration of the letter A" (*akāroddeśaka*), the instruction here is as follows: the letter A is suchness (*tathatā*), signifying the unstruck sound (*anāhataśabda*). It is the heart of the Buddhas, the secret, and the reality (*tattva*). And it is said in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, the supreme syllable.
[It continues: "This mantra is the utterance," and so forth.

One should recite the mantra ending with "abhinnāṅgam. All of this is to be understood as having been brought there [into this context] from the explanation of the fourfold reality of mantra (*mantratattva*) found in the verse that sets forth the *bodhicitta* at the time of the junctions (*sandhyā*).

Now, the number of recitations for this vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*) over the course of a day and night is established. Although the venerable master [Nāgārjuna] taught the recitation by relying on the mandalas of Agni and the others—stating that "the recitation of Pāṇḍaravāsī and the rest is proclaimed," and so forth—nevertheless, according to the tradition set forth in the *Sūtaka* composed by the venerable Āryadeva, the yogin must first meditate on the wind-mandala in sequence. In this regard, the procedure is as follows:

Emerging from the left nostril, there is the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi within the wind-maṇḍala; he has the nature of wind, and the wind-maṇḍala consists of greenish-black rays. Herein, a distinction is stated:

the movement [of the breath] is observed to follow the sequence of the two transits of the moon and the sun. Consequently, according to the astronomical treatises (*jyotiṣika-śāstra*), the worldly convention is based on sixty *daṇḍas*; by relying on that, one quarter (*pāda*) constitutes the fourth division of a single *daṇḍa*.
Fifteen *pala* of water for this [measure], multiplied by four, becomes sixty *pala* of water; by this, one *daṇḍa* is established. With one *pala* of water there are six breaths;
thus, in one quarter-hour (*pāda*) there are ninety breaths.
Furthermore, by multiplying this [number] fourfold and adding one *daṇḍa*, there are three hundred and sixty breaths (*śvāsa*).

According to this division, established by the rotation of two and a half *daṇḍas*, and by making two and a half quarters through the fourth part of the rotation of counting, there are two hundred and twenty-five breaths for each of the [five yoginīs] beginning with Pāṇḍarā.
How many *pala* of water does this correspond to?
In this regard, multiplied by these four factors, the total sum is nine hundred and four;

thus, the arrangement of qualities for each production is established across twenty-four circumambulations. With twenty-four circumambulations, there are twenty-four transitions; therefore, a mandala of ninety-six [deities] is intended for the assembly.

Is it not the case that, having attained the vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*) through the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) in the *Hevajratantra*, the Blessed One demonstrated sixty-four mandalas—sixty-four by means of the night’s thirty-two dandas and the day’s sixty-four dandas? Here, the word "danda" is a synonym for "mandala," and sixty-four dandas are spoken of with the intention of joining them to the four wheels (*cakra*).
Thus, the question arises: how can there be an equivalent arrangement [of these] together with the twenty-fourfold division of circumambulations (*parikrama*) in the *Śrīsamāja*?
This is the superior view favored by the Hevajrins.

It should be understood that the establishment of the synonyms—*parikrama*, *maṇḍalaparivarta*, and *paripāṭi*—refers to the circumambulation among the four [types of practitioners] by a wise practitioner (*vijñabhāvaka*). How so?
Here it is said: "It is indeed the case that there are nine hundred breaths in the course of two and a half *daṇḍas*;

that a transition (*saṃkrānti*) is made by means of nine hundred breaths does not hold together. Why? Because of the principle that just as there is an external arrangement by means of the *daṇḍa*, so too is there an internal one."
And the sequence of transits is indeed different;
that is stated as follows:

having subtracted three-quarters of four *pānīyapala*s from sixty *pānīyapala*s by means of a single staff, fifty-six *pānīyapala*s plus one-quarter of a *pānīyapala* remain situated in one *maṇḍala*.
Where [the rule states] "56 / pāda 1," having multiplied this by four, two hundred and twenty-five palas of water [are required].
In the definitive sense (*nītārtha*):
when this very [number] is made sixfold and multiplied by the calculation of the moments of arising (*pratyutpāda-gaṇanā*), [it results in... 225.
There are one thousand three hundred and fifty breaths; this is the total. By this, for a practitioner of the *Sāmājika* [system], there would be four *daṇḍas* per quarter-turn (*parikrama*).
For a practitioner of *Hevajra*, by the fourth part of this—namely, one *daṇḍa* minus a quarter (*pāda*) per quarter—the breaths of one *maṇḍala* are 337 and two quarters (*pāda*).

According to this much of the text, having reached the time of half a watch (*ardhayāmikā*), the flow of wind through the nostrils in the sequence of the four *maṇḍalas* establishes sixteen transitions (*saṃkrānti*); such is the opinion of the *Hevajra* practitioners.

By this very same method, such an arrangement is to be understood by the yogin of vajra-recitation in the other second nostril; by this, one watch (prahara) is completed. Furthermore, whatever explanation has been given for one watch is to be understood by the wise regarding the subsequent watches as well.
As for the nine hundred that were specified, through twenty-four circumambulations,
it becomes two myriads, one thousand, and sixteen hundred; that is,
when the stated nine hundred are multiplied by the calculation of twenty-four circumambulations, it results in two myriads, one thousand, and sixteen hundred.

In this regard, where there is his "water-vessel" (pānīyapala), and where, in the case of a single staff (*daṇḍa*), sixty staves are established through the arrangement of the qualities of the instrument—

having made six watches (*prahara*) by means of fifteen staves in the *Śrīsamāja*, and six watches at night— by dividing these into half-watches, those twenty-four circumambulations (*parikrama*) designated for a day and night are to be understood according to the distinction between the activities (*karman*) such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth.

The variety of teachings concerning the different sequences of the yoga-tantras has been taught here by the Blessed One together with the Yoginī-tantras; there is no distinction regarding vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*). Therefore, the establishment of the external and internal timings is as follows: having divided the day and night into eight watches (*prahara*) by means of sixty *daṇḍas*, each watch consists of seven and a half *daṇḍas*.
How many breaths occur?

In that [period] where there is one *pala* of water for him, and where this very [period] is multiplied by eight—here, however, a distinction must be stated: from the sequence of the staff of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-daṇḍakrama*) up to the end of the month of Śrāvaṇa, it is pervaded by the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana-saṃkrānti*). Having thus divided it into two staffs, there is an increase at night and a decrease during the day.

Subsequently, from the beginning of the month of Māgha up to the end of the month of Āṣāḍha, it is pervaded by the southern solstice; having thus divided it into two staffs, there is an increase during the day.
In the world, a decrease is observed during the night between the two transits (*saṃkrānti*).
The two months of Āśvina and Caitra are prescribed [as the period of equilibrium];
because of their state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), there is neither transit nor increase for the two *daṇḍas*.
Although all of this has been explained according to the sequence of the staff (daṇḍakrama),
nevertheless, it remains established as a fixed rule that without sixteen hundred and twenty thousand breaths in a single day and night, a correct thorough knowledge does not arise externally.
By this it is meant:

the knowledge of time through the sequence of the staff [method] of the astronomical treatises, and the knowledge of time through the sequence of the staff [method] of dependent origination—these two are not even slightly contradictory when combined with the knowledge of internal time according to both systems.
Others, however, have different limbs [of the system].

With respect to the six maṇḍalas, it flows for one and a half revolutions in the first cavity; subsequently, having transferred [to the next], it flows for one and a half revolutions with respect to the six maṇḍalas in the second cavity. Thus, by this sequence of explanation, the acceptance of the thorough knowledge of the internal and external results in exactly sixteen transitions of the *sampuṭa* in one day and night—this is merely some triviality.
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the four moments of the junctions (*saṃdhyā*) during the movement through each individual maṇḍala, he says "vidyā" and so forth.
"Vidyā" refers to Pāṇḍarā; the "maṇḍala of the fire-eater" (Agni) is its meaning. The "method" (*naya*) is the sequential rule (*ānupūrvvikā nītiḥ*) pertaining to her.

The meaning of the phrase "the performance of this rite according to rule through the practice of the four junctions" (*anuṣṭhānacatuḥsandhyaprayogataḥ*) is as follows: when the flow of the wind-mandala has ceased in the nostril, there subsequently occurs the entry of the fire-mandala; the realization of a subtle moment between these two is called the "four junctions" (*catuḥsandhya*) of the four mandalas, by way of both practice and realization.

For this very reason, it is established that one should recite the mantra—whether it be the three-syllabled one—together with the wind, as an inseparable part [of it], and not effect a separation from the mantra.
"The target" (*lakṣyam*) means that which is to be characterized; "by the number of syllables" (*akṣarasamkhyayā*) means by the enumeration of the various conceptualizations.
Regarding the phrase "external recitation" (*bāhyajāpam*) and so forth:
the yogin should abandon—that is, completely relinquish—external recitation, which is to say, vocal recitation.
It is an obstacle to cultivation;
it is caused by obstacles to the cultivation of vajra-recitation.
The meaning of the mantra is the Blessed One, the Vajrī.
That meaning of the mantra is the vajra-recitation; by means of that, he himself is the Blessed One. He is the Vajrin, whose intrinsic nature is Vajrasattva;
indeed, he is the Vajrātman.
Because there is no difference between the mantra and the deity. The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "however. How should one recite?
It is intended that one does not perform vocal recitation, which is the utterance of the mantra.
Explaining this very point by means of an analogy, he says:
"One who has obtained an elephant," and so forth; having obtained the elephant, one would immediately, at that very moment, search for the elephant's tracks.
Is it not true that one who seeks an elephant searches for the elephant's footprint?
Therefore, there is the "mantra-body" (*mantramūrti*).
A "mantra-body" is a body produced or accomplished by means of the three-syllabled mantra.

Therefore, the yogin himself directly [perceives] that which is called the "indirect indication" (upalakṣā) conjoined with the vajra-recitation; what else could he seek? It is established that he does not perform the utterance of mantras.
Here, the word *api* has the sense of "furthermore" (*punar-arthe*), as in the phrase "api ca" and so forth.
The indeclinable word "eva" (here rendered as *avyaya*) functions as a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). O Vajradhṛk, a certain person endowed with the three conjunctions—
the practitioner of mantra possessing the three *satvas*— should perform the observation of the entry, abiding, and exit of the wind.
Through the yoga of practice that is respectful, uninterrupted, and long-lasting,
a certain person becomes Vajradhṛk himself.
[The passage beginning with] "invocation" (āvāhana), etc., [follows].
This is the summary.
It is made clear by the detailed explanation beginning with "by means of invocation and entry," and so forth.
It is stated that the application of the mantra is performed during haste, obstruction, or weeping.
The application of the three syllables to the three words should be performed according to their respective fitness.
As for the passage beginning with "at the root of the ear" and ending with "thus,
in the *Guhyasandhyā*, the subtle yoga has been revealed," it is easy to understand from the very root text.
Regarding "meditation is incomparable," and so forth:
that which has no equal (tulā) is "incomparable" (atula).
What would happen then after having recited the mantra that is its equal?
The one hundred and sixteen winds dissolve into the mind.

When the wind has dissolved into the mind, then, through the sequence of entry into the nostrils and so forth, the practitioner who is engaged in the means of accomplishment shall achieve the very clear vision of the fourfold mandala consisting of the five Tathāgatas.
For that yogin, the three worlds—the body, speech, and mind—will undoubtedly be accomplished as non-dual (*ālīka*).
Having clearly explained the visualization of the four mandalas, he now says "six," and so forth, in order to show that the remaining twenty thousand breaths have dissolved back into the mind.

The three-syllable mantra, which has the nature of wind, consists of five colors and is essentially the five gnoses; these very four mandalas serve as the cause for the two types of false appearances of gnosis.
"From this, arising from knowledge" means that which has arisen correctly as the residual breath (*śeṣaśvāsa*).
"Having recited it twenty thousand times in one month" amounts to six hundred thousand [recitations].
Regarding the phrase "having paid homage to Vajrasattva," what is the meaning?

Vajrasattva is the nature of the three syllables; having propitiated and meditated upon him, that yogin succeeds and, having attained the nature of the unreality of body, speech, and mind, becomes equal to Vajradhara. This is the meaning of "on which full moon? In response to the doubt as to whether such a yogin must observe vows and so forth or not, [the text says] "not for him," and so on.

The recitation of mantras consisting of verbal utterance, the retention [of breath] through haṭhayoga, or the restraint of the vital winds—all these cease; even other various activities such as bathing, eating, and so forth need not be performed. Rather, it is said that they are accomplished through *vajrajāpa* alone, beginning with the phrase "by means of the meaning of the letter *ya*" and so on.

When the wind-mandala transformed from the syllable *yam* is set in motion, whatever is to be done—namely, the fourfold ritual actions beginning with pacification (*śāntika*)—the activity of the world is accomplished precisely through the triad beginning with the syllable *ra*; this is the same meaning as previously stated. "In fire," and so forth;
at the time of half a watch (*ardhayāmikavelā*).
"At the time of half a watch (*ardhapraharavelā*), two activities each persist.

This means that while the wind-maṇḍala is primarily flowing, two activities are presented; however, since the other three maṇḍalas are also possible there, it is possible for two activities to occur by way of being secondary (*gauṇa*) and primary (*mukhya*). There is no fault here because of the principle that "where there is one, there are four. He states the result:
From "pūjāprāya" and so forth up to "nirvikalpaikadhīmataḥ," this is easy to understand from the very beginning.
From "vāgvajrasya" and so forth...
Having performed the observation of the wind of the speech-vajra together with its support, by means of the differentiation of the three types of gnosis.

The meaning of this is explained as follows: One should apply the mind solely to the three aspects—entry, abiding, and emergence—of the wind of the three syllables within the nostrils, which is the vajra-mind (*cittavajra*) that serves as the cause for the vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*) that is the means for directly realizing [the truth], and which is characterized by the arising of the three gnoses (*jñāna*). Thus, the word "solely" (*mātra*) is used in a restrictive sense, meaning that the wind becomes entirely dissolved in the mind alone.
By this, when stability of mind is attained, the practitioner attains the mastery of speech and the mastery of mind.
By this it is meant:
having fully attained mastery of mind, one becomes a lord of the eight stages.
And it was stated in the *Anuttarasandhi*:

"By means of the yoga of a beginner (*ādikarmika*), one may attain the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). Therefore, this very instruction for those who practice the meditation on *vajrajapa* has been written here at the outset.
He states the definition of the disciple:
"But one who is disrespectful toward the guru is a rogue," and so forth;
or one who is arrogant regarding the mantra, or one whose speech is... [39b4] (D179b6, P413a4).
Because of being devoted to evil.
The one to be grasped is to be favored by the instruction on vajra-recitation; the rest of the phrase is easy to understand.
"Girīndra," and so forth.

Having obtained the most beneficial instructions through the grace of the Guru, he is not merely liberated; is he not liberated by the instruction alone? He would indeed become a Buddha, and moreover, he does not go to the six states of miserable rebirth (*apāyagati*).
By this, even though he is not yet liberated, he is designated as "liberated.
Thus ends the *Yogimanoharā* commentary on the *Vajrajāpa*.
In the *Piṇḍīkrama* and the *Vajrajāpakrama*, the identity of the three gnoses (*jñānatraya*) was established separately.
Now, in order to establish their non-differentiated form, he says:
"Having prostrated to the Great Vajra," and so forth.
It is "Great-Vajra" because it is both great and a vajra; one should prostrate to that Great-Vajra, which is the nature of the Great Emptiness— this is the grammatical connection.
Those very [beings] have Vajrasattva and others as their leaders.
"Vajra" is emptiness; he whose intention (*satva*) is directed toward that is "Sattva. He alone is the nature of great emptiness.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), Akṣobhya and the others are included. Among these, he is the leader by virtue of being their father.
Furthermore, this is the sequence of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*); the unreal body, speech, and mind that have been explained are denoted here by the term "self" (*sva*).

Their *adhiṣṭhāna* is the accomplishment of the form of the bliss of non-apprehension through the state of mutual non-separation; the sequence by which that occurs is the *svādhiṣṭhānakrama*. The word "ca" (*and*) serves to fill out the meter.
It will be spoken—that is, it will be explained—by me, Nāgārijuna, out of compassion (*kṛpā*), that is, through the mercy that takes the Dharma as its object.
First, regarding "in accordance with the generation stage" and so forth:
first of all, he has received initiation;

that is, he has been consecrated according to the sequence of the ritual procedures through the master’s initiation and the others. He is one who understands the intended meaning of the four types of tantras.
"One who knows the Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Yoginī Tantras," and so forth; one who has attained the isolation of body, speech, and mind through the stage of Vajra-recitation.

Therefore, for this very reason, the term "retainer of the scriptures" (*śrutidhara*) refers to the inclusion of the jewel-like person by virtue of being a retainer of the scriptures; "resolute confidence in the two truths" means one who has resolute confidence in the two truths of conventional truth and ultimate truth. Regarding the passage beginning with "having propitiated the Vajra Guru," the meaning is as follows: previously, the instruction on the stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*) was heard through the explanation of the master (*śāstravyākhyāna*);
now, in order to realize that through the explanation of the disciple (*śiṣyavyākhyāna*), one must propitiate the Vajra Guru—this is the connection.

"Therefore" means that because of such service and propitiation, the Guru becomes satisfied. To the satisfied Guru—meaning one who has been rendered well-disposed within the center of the *cakra* by the enjoyment of the five objects of desire—he says:
"One should perform great worship of the assembly," and so forth, with the following passage beginning with "Immediately thereafter."

Immediately after the enjoyment of the five sensory pleasures, the teacher should reveal to the disciple that instruction on self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna) which has been received from the mouth of the guru— that is, uttered from the mouths of the lineage of gurus.
In that case, by what sequence?

From the words "thereafter" (*tataḥ*) onwards, having received [the initiations] from the garland initiation (*mālābhiṣeka*) up to the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*), the Vajra-Guru should subsequently establish the reality (*tatva*) within the *vajramaṇi* for these two initiations and for the wisdom initiation (*prajñābhiṣeka*) to be described hereafter. Why should he establish the reality after having sprinkled [the disciple]? Because of the statement: "Of all illusions (*māyā*), the illusion of a woman (*strīmāyā*) alone is preeminent."
This distinction between the three types of gnosis is clearly perceived right here;
therefore, by means of the master initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), the "grasped" gnosis (*grāhyajñāna*) is taught, and its antidote is the "gnosis of light" (*ālokajñāna*).
By means of the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*), the "grasper" gnosis (*grāhakajñāna*) is taught, and its antidote is the "appearance of light" (*ālokābhāsa*).

Having taught the two types of knowledge during the night in their proper sequence, one might object: "Since the instruction on self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) ought to be presented here, would it not be more appropriate to teach the consecration of wisdom (*prajñābhiṣeka*)?
How then is this explanation of the two consecrations [justified], and what is its true nature? This is true.
Since that cannot be demonstrated without a sequential order, he says:
"The teacher will demonstrate to the disciple the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), which is characterized by the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*)."

For this purpose, with these verses— beginning with "In these... and ending with "Homage to you who have attained the selfless state, being without support because of the aforementioned porosity and so forth"— one should praise the Guru, whose essential nature is inseparable from the three types of knowledge.
"Regarding 'there is no hollowness' and so forth:
there is no state of being hollow in the body;
it is like a rainbow in the sky."
The illustration is by virtue of being endowed with the colors of five rays.
"Āmaya" and so forth:
*āmaya* means disease.
"Is not impure," and so forth, is easy to understand.
"Like the moon in water, ungraspable," and so forth:
because it cannot withstand analysis, it does not have the nature of reality.

Because it is within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), it is not false; by this, it should be understood as being like the moon reflected in water. Likewise, the meaning is that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is non-reliant upon any phenomena.
"Free from ego-grasping" (*anahaṃkāra*) and "free from delusion" (*nirmoha*) are easy to understand.

Therefore, because of the abandonment of the conceptualization of the two appearances, let there be salutation to the objectless (*nirālambana*); let there be homage. By this very sequence, the explanation of the term "objectless" should also be understood by the wise in the verses to be recited hereafter.
The words beginning with "always" (*sadā*) and so forth are easy to understand.

Regarding the words beginning with "you manifest" (*vikurvasi*), it means that through the illusion-like samādhi, there is an analogy (*upamā*)—that is, a similarity—with an illusion, namely, with an illusory body.
The analysis of the compound is: "this samādhi is like an illusion.
Therefore, this is its specific qualification.

By the term *maharddhyā* (by great supernatural power), it is meant that one has entered into that [samādhi] which is "devoid of manifoldness" (*nirnnānātva*), where manifoldness—meaning conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and discursive thought (*vikalpa*)—has departed.
"Thus," and so forth.

Having thus praised the Vajra Master with his true qualities—that is, with his qualities as they truly are—one should request him for the sake of hearing [the teaching] by means of this verse that is about to be spoken:
"O Omniscient One, mass of primordial wisdom," and so on.
"Sandoha" means a collection.
Regarding "the wheel of existence" (*bhavacakra*):
existence itself is the wheel, because one wanders through the five destinies according to the manner of a wheel.
The purifier of that [defilement]:

"Today," on this very day, "by means of the jewel of exposition"—that is, by means of the jewel of exposition concerning conventional truth—grant me, O Lord, clarity of mind, beginning with the words "at your feet" and so forth; this is easy to understand. "Thus," and so on:
having heard those words of his disciple, which were characterized by being "skilled in entreaty"—meaning primarily devoted to the act of requesting—[the Master spoke].
"Compassion" is easily understood.
Regarding "then one should begin the self-consecration" (*svādhiṣṭhāna*),
the Guru begins the explanation of self-consecration.
"Self-consecration," and so forth.

What is the vision of the truth (*satyadarśana*) of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*)? It is the collection of entities such as trees, mountains, rivers, and oceans; this is the conventional. Without this, the realization of the truth does not occur at all.
And likewise, the venerable master Candrakīrti said:
"Do not destroy conventional reality, for it is established by the world.
The vision of this [reality] is the vision of the three bodies (trikāya), which consist of the three gnoses and are composed of the body of non-dual knowledge.
The passage beginning with "gurupāda" is easy to understand.
Regarding the phrase "by whom" and so forth:
it means by whichever practitioner [the instruction] is not obtained or attained from the presence of the guru.
The instruction on the stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) resides within one's own body.

For that yogin, exertion and effort spent upon the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) found in the *sūtras*, *tantras*, and ritual manuals (*kalpas*) are in vain and fruitless; "exertion" and "effort" are synonyms. And it is said in the *Caturdevīparipṛcchā-mahāyogatantra*: "In the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma of the Great Sage..."
"Those who do not know reality are indeed all fruitless.

Regarding the "stage of self-consecration" (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*) and so forth: having obtained and attained the stage of self-consecration from the Vajra Guru by means of hearing the explanation for the disciple regarding that which was taught during the Wisdom Initiation (*prajñābhiṣeka*)—namely, the gnosis of great emptiness—one becomes composed of all Buddhas, having the very nature of all Buddhas.
For this very reason, the Lord of the three worlds attains Buddhahood in this very life— in his present birth— just as it occurs when all doubt has been eliminated;
thus it is obtained.
"And the samādhi of self-consecration, as well as the state of luminosity," and so forth.
The word "ca" (and) serves to complete the meter.

Just as that is the state of the two truths, so too is it the state of ultimate truth; thus the two truths are proclaimed in the world of yogins. With this, he says "by way of the distinction between result and cause" in order to demonstrate the relationship of cause and effect between the two truths already mentioned, both in direct and reverse order.
This luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) is first described as the fruit of conventional truth;
for luminosity is indeed attained through the sequence of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).

Therefore, the Vajra Master should first demonstrate self-consecration as the causal state and explain it according to this very order. Thus, in order to show the relationship between cause and fruit even for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) by means of the elements such as earth and so forth, he says:
The earth element dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire;
fire dissolves into the subtle element; and wind dissolves into the mind.
The mind dissolves into the mental factors, and the mental factors into ignorance;
that too goes into the luminous state—this is cessation within the three realms of existence.
Likewise, by reversing these two, there is a causal relationship consisting of four voids (*śūnyacatuṣṭaya*), which will be explained [in the passage] beginning with "not independent" (*asvatantra*).
"Not independent" means that the entire world is dependent upon causes and conditions.

The mind of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the great emptiness (*mahāśūnya*), which is the form of the effect; its cause is the clear light (*prabhāsvara*). What is the nature of this clear light? It has the characteristic of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyalakṣaṇa*). [Objection: Is it not the case that the cause of the result, which is the form of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), cannot be the clear light?
[Response: From the clear light comes the great emptiness, and from that arises skillful means (*upāya*); from that, wisdom (*prajñā*) is produced, and from that, wind (*pavana*) arises.
From wind arises fire; from fire arises water;
and from water the earth is born. This is the origin of sentient beings. Thus it is established that there is no cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
And likewise, the venerable Āryadeva says: "The four elements beginning with earth, as well as the four voids—these eight categories should be known as the causes of destruction and arising.
By this, the following is stated:
What is the distinction between an ordinary person and a practitioner for whom all things are like an illusion?
It is not known.
This is the distinction of the practitioner from ordinary persons: for they, like a magician, do not perceive [the existence of] entities that are not actually apprehended.
They do not adhere to them as real.
However, those who, like foolish people, adhere to them as being real are called "fools" because of their erroneous adherence.
And it is said in another place: "Nothing is to be removed from this..."
"Nothing at all is to be added, and nothing at all is to be removed; by seeing reality as it truly is, one who sees reality is liberated."
In both direct and reverse order, the relationship between cause and fruit is exactly the same;
nevertheless, having encountered [the state] with and without latent tendencies (*savāsana-nirvāsana*), the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) inquires out of his own understanding.
Demonstrating this very point again, he says:
"By which," and so forth:
by which mind of mine, not fully understood through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), fools are attached to phenomena and have fallen into bondage.
Where?
Transmigration in *saṃsāra* means wandering from one state of existence to another; that is to say, from one destination to a different destination.
By means of that mind—the illusion-like samādhi—having thoroughly understood the intrinsic nature of phenomena, yogins have gone to the destination of the Sugatas.

Thus, regarding this distinguished mind, no one arises here, nor does anyone die; with reference to the mind of the yogin perfected by these two phrases, the statement that "the essence of speech is to be known as abiding in the form and appearance of the mind" and so forth should be understood.
With reference to the mind of the yogin not yet perfected, these two phrases demonstrate duality.
To clarify this, he says in two verses:
"Through the yoga of the winds," and so forth:
without the cause of vajra-recitation, the stability of the mind—its very nature—is not grasped;
it is not attained.
Rather, it is through yoga alone that the yogi attains the effect of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).
By this, the form of the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*), which is non-different from the three cognitions,
is expressed by the word "of the mind" (*cittāt*).

Due to a lack of familiarity with the illusion-like meditative absorption, and through the conjunction of wind and consciousness, the fundamental natures characterized by passion, dispassion, and so forth—
which possess an unwholesome intrinsic nature—
come into being.
Why? Because it has its cause in primordial nature (*prakṛti*); therefore, from that primordial nature comes karma, and from that arises birth.
By this principle, the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), not knowing the true state of existence, undertakes the grasping of birth.
And so it is said in the *Tantra*: "These ten unwholesome [actions]..."

The meaning that "those devoid of knowledge perform the paths of action" has been explained by the author of the Sūtra. Thus, sentient beings [act so] due to their lack of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).

Without attaining the thorough knowledge of one's own mind as it truly is, one imagines it to be empty, void, devoid of "I" and "mine," and so forth—such as [the notions of] purity and so on—and thus experiences suffering in beginningless saṃsāra. Therefore, that very mind which is like an illusion is non-different from the threefold consciousness; it is the realization of light produced by the two lights, free from the two appearances, and possesses the form of the deity characterized by the previously explained consecration of the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*).
The form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is born—that is, it arises—for the yogin.
Therefore, and so forth:

for this reason, this entire world—the triple realm (*traidhātuka*) consisting of both the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*)—is here said to be like an illusion (*māyopama*).
The practitioner established in the illusion-like samādhi perceives everything that is spoken of within the three realms as being just like an illusion. And it is said in the *Anuttarasandhi*:
"And the one who perceives the three appearances is established on the ten stages," beginning with "form and feeling indeed," and so forth.
That form is non-different internally and externally, that everything is merely illusion and nothing else— this [passage] is clear by virtue of the previous explanation.

Having thus explained the illusory body (*māyādeha*), [the author] speaks in response to the question of how one might recognize it: "The practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) should recognize the illusory body through examples such as a reflection in a mirror,
and the [illusory] colors through a rainbow."
Pervasiveness is [illustrated] by the moon in water, by virtue of its being endowed with rays such as white light;
for even though the moon is one and the same, it is seen in various vessels when accompanied by water.
In the same way, the pervasiveness of the illusory body (*māyādeha*)—in what stainless, pure mirror [is it seen]? This and more is easily understood.

"Vajrasattva is well-painted" means: Vajrasattva is qualified as "well-painted" (sucitrita), that is, beautifully depicted. How so? Just as from a painted canvas, because there is no differentiation [of parts], a single-form cognition arises.
"In the same way, Vajrasattva is well-painted.
And what is he like? "Endowed with the excellence of all aspects," and so forth, in detail.

Although this form has been more clearly depicted by the Noble Ones, nevertheless, for the sake of those of dull intellect, I shall state the summarized meaning of the entire instruction on the stages of consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Here it is said:

[The deity] has a white lotus and moon as a seat; upon that, he is white in color, two-armed, single-faced, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, his head adorned with matted locks (jaṭā), his sprout-like hands placed in the gesture of meditative concentration (samādhimudrā), embraced by Vajradhātvīśvarī, or else having the form of the empowerment inseparable from the three vajras, possessing the nature of five-colored rays like a rainbow of Indra, endowed with false habitual tendencies, a mental body (manomayakāya) that is transparent, and having attained the moment of "rubbing" (vimarda) as established by the third initiation of the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñānābhiṣeka);
he is of the nature of the perception of light (ālokopalabdha).

For those of superior capacity, through the yoga of instantaneous appearance, the Vajra Guru should show the Great Emptiness Wisdom—the Sambhogakāya of the Buddhas, possessing the thirty-two major marks and a body adorned with the eighty minor signs—which is to be personally realized within. In what [mirror] and for which excellent disciple should he show it?
Regarding this very [wisdom], its characteristic is called "self-consecration" (*svādhiṣṭhāna*); that is explained therein.
And it has been said by the venerable Āryadeva:
"Just as a form endowed with all its parts shines forth most clearly in the reflection of a mirror,
so too the body of Vajradhara always possesses the eighty secondary marks and the primary marks."
"This very [body]," and so forth:
"to be perceived" (samlakṣyā) means that which is to be correctly characterized (samyak-lakṣaṇīyā) as having the nature of a body consisting of illusory knowledge (*māyāmaya-jñāna*).
"And that is the enjoyment body" (*sāmbhogika-kāya*) means that the body resembling an illusion is the enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*).
It is accessible to the lords of the ten stages;

"that very [body]" and so forth refers to the previously mentioned *saṃbhogakāya*. However, because it is born separately in various realms of existence (*gati*), it is designated as a "gandharva-being" with reference to the minds of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The passage beginning with "vajrakāya" is easy to understand. Regarding "ātma" and so forth:
"sarvaśauritvam" means the state of being all-pervading heroism, which is to say, the form of the Great Vajradhara.
The passage beginning with "tasmāt" is clear; he speaks in order to demonstrate that one should perform everything by means of the illusion-like body (māyopamakāya).

Regarding the passage beginning with "the application of mantra and mudrā," etc.: if one desires to perform the application of mantra and mudrā, the conceptualization of mandalas and so forth, or to construct mandalas and the like, by relying upon conventional reality (saṃvṛti), then one should at all times perform all of that—including the rites of bali and homa—exclusively in a form resembling an illusion (māyopama); thus there is no fault. Likewise, one should perform pacifying (śāntika), enriching (pauṣṭika), subjugating (vaśya), and malevolent (abhicāruka) rites entirely as if they were like a rainbow (indrāyudha). As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra*: "One obtains a body resembling an Indra’s bow through the cultivation of reality."
This is its meaning: "Indra" refers to Śakra, and "weapon" (āyudha) refers to a bow (dhanuḥ) by way of conventional designation;
thus, the meaning is "Indra’s bow.

What is that Indra-bow? It is characterized by the colors of five rays. Just as Indra’s bow appears clearly in the expanse of the sky through a variety of colors, in exactly the same way, the Saṃbhogakāya—
The meaning is "perceived.
Regarding the phrase "erotic sentiment and so forth": this refers to the enjoyment of the erotic sentiment and the like, as well as the practice of singing, instrumental music, and so on.
"When it acts, then [it is] like the moon in water"—
the meaning of this has already been explained by the preceding [passage], and is therefore easy to understand.
[This applies to] "form," "sound," and so forth.

Regarding form and sound, the activity of the eye and so forth occurs; and because one thinks, "form is grasped by the eye," the meaning is that the objects of the eye and so forth are seen to possess a resemblance like an illusion (*māyā*), similar to an illusory body (*māyādeha*). What is the use of saying more? The rest is easy to understand. [The passage beginning with] "and the reflection in a mirror" refers to the twelve examples, such as the mirror and so forth.

The illusory body (*māyādeha*) is to be understood by the advanced practitioner. It is similar to a magical illusion (*indrajāla*); just as a magician creates elephants, horses, and so forth through magic, so too the yogi who perceives the body as being like a magical illusion and comparable to a conjuration is remembered as one who has attained lordship over the worlds.
