And so it was said in the *Jñānavajrasamuccayamahāyogatantra* regarding the *Sūtakas*: "Illuminating this very illusion-like samādhi, he said: 'The union of mind and mental factors is the samādhi of great bliss; it is characterized by such similes as illusion. All Tathāgatas, Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, are like illusions, like the moon in water, and like reflections.'"

The meditative absorption of great bliss (*mahāsukha-samādhi*) is characterized by twelve examples of illusion: a mirage, a dream, an echo, a city of the *gandharvas*, a magician’s trick, Indra’s bow (the rainbow), lightning, a bubble, a water-bubble, and a reflection in a mirror.
The meaning of these twelve examples is explained as follows:

it is "illusion" (*māyā*) because of its causal efficiency; a "mirage" (*marīci*) because of its falsity; and a "city of the *gandharvas*" (*gandharvanagara*) because it appears in an indefinite location.
Indra’s bow [the rainbow] is [an illusion] by virtue of its manifold colors;
a reflection in a mirror by virtue of its clarity; the moon in water by virtue of its pervasiveness; an echo by virtue of appearing in another location;
a dream by virtue of being mere cognition; and a shadow by virtue of being devoid of flesh.
A mass of clouds, by virtue of being the cause for a great roar; lightning, by virtue of persisting for only a moment;
and a bubble, by virtue of vanishing as soon as it arises.
"Is seen," and so forth:

Just as a magical illusion (*indrajāla*) is both seen and touched, so too the world is always like an illusion; thus, the world, with its forms, touches, and so on, is proclaimed at all times to be comparable to a magical illusion.

Furthermore, there is no perception [of objects] in the state of conventional truth; the multitude of existing things is not perceived. That which exists as the true nature (*dharmatā*) has the nature of truth and the nature of conventional truth; that which is the *dharmatā* has been thus described. And it is stated in the *Mahāyānaviṃśatikā*: "When a magician always produces [an illusion], at that time, the illusory phenomena do not exist; for that is indeed the *dharmatā* of illusory phenomena."
Having relied upon this, that which is the nature of conventional truth is proclaimed to be like an illusion (*māyā*).

Relying on worldly convention, the Blessed One gave the teaching of the world as being like an illusion; however, in the state of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is established that even the linguistic usage of "that which is taught" and "the teaching" does not exist.
To demonstrate this very point once more, he says:
"Whatever it may be," and so forth:
whatever form, sound, or other [object] has as its path— that is, as its range— the sense-faculties such as the eye, and whose nature would thus be reached or attained,
that very thing [is established] by way of its own-nature (*svabhāva*).
"By means of the yoga of non-meditative equipoise" refers to the nature of the enjoyment body (*sambhogadeha*), which is like an illusion according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Regarding "non-meditative equipoise":

it is either equipoised during a state that is not [formally] equipoised; or else, "yoga" is that which is established or produced by the "unequal"—namely, the three types of knowledge consisting of light and so forth, which serve as the antidotes to the apprehended object and so on—and this yoga is characterized by the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) inseparable from the three vajras.
By this, one should understand that [the practitioner] attains the nature of an illusory body (*māyādeha*) consisting of all Buddhas.

How could it consist of all Buddhas? It is because its characteristic is self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), and since it is something to be realized even by the Lords of the Ten Stages, it is appropriate to speak of it as the form of a Bodhisattva who is a Lord of the Ten Stages.
This is true.
According to the scriptural teaching that on the tenth stage Bodhisattvas are indeed Buddhas, but not yet Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*samyaksambuddha*),
the explanation of the phrases "everywhere," "in all respects," and so forth, is easy to understand. Now, demonstrating the pervasiveness of the illusory body (*māyādeha*), he says:
Whether walking, standing, and so forth—
because of his greatness, that yogin is a "Great Being" (mahāsattva);
he is the ultimate state consisting of all happiness.
Because he is free from the latencies of all the sufferings of saṃsāra, he consists of all happiness.
He is the Lord because he manifests within the three realms by virtue of having the nature of Vajrasattva.
For this very reason, the yogin—having entered the illusion-like samādhi—obtains and attains dwellings, food, drink, and so forth, from space in an instant, that is, without delay.
"May they become," and so forth.

Those practitioners of mantra who possess the nature of all Buddhas and who cut through the entire web of conceptual constructions of existence—may they become teachers in the most excellent world; that is, teachers in the most excellent, supreme world.
By whom is that yogin worshipped? The meaning is: by all the sounds. Having done what? Having prostrated again and again at all times.
"Yathā" and so forth;
he states an example:
just as the course of worldly affairs proceeds toward the Teacher, the Perfectly Awakened One, who is one who seeks the welfare [of beings].

In the same way, for the great yogin as well, because of the inclusion of the knowledge consisting of the universe— since his body, which consists of the knowledge whose nature is the world, has been fully grasped—
it is as stated in the passage beginning with "it does not exist."
Whatever is born of the universe—such as all objects, words, and so forth—is certainly not something unachievable;
for it is known and understood by Vajrasattva through his illusory body that everything is indeed achievable. All mudrās are those who possess great bliss.

Therefore, the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "the afflictions" (*kleśā*) and so forth is that all these [afflictions], whose intrinsic nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), are themselves established for the yogi through the application of the aspect of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
The "paths of action" (*karmapatha*) refer to the ten unwholesome actions and so forth.
By the word "body" (*deha*), birth (*janma*) is intended.
How so?
It has been said: "From affliction comes karma, from that comes birth; for this very reason, there are both agents and fruits.
Since the world arises from this great emptiness which is luminous, they are called "agents."

When the fruit of the realization of these truths is certain, then the yogi should understand that [all things] are like the example of an illusory body (*māyādeha*), resembling a mirage, a dream, or a city of the Gandharvas—this is what is meant by "this" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "their illusions are conquered by the physician":

for those yogis who have not attained the illusion-like samādhi, various kinds of diseases arise; for those who have attained the illusion-like samādhi, their diseases are conquered by the physician of illusion—this is the meaning.

The passage beginning with "The instruction on self-consecration" (*svādhiṣṭhānopadeśa*) and ending with "from the great fear of the ocean of suffering" (*duḥkhārṇṇavamahābhayāt*) is easy to understand from the root text itself. He now states the characterization of the disciple:

"He who is smeared with the garland of egoism," and so forth, is also clear; "one whose speech is truthful," and so forth—truthful speech means one who is secluded and reflective. He who performs the hearing, recitation, and so on under a single guru.

In some places he may be called "pure" (sāttvika), and in others "endowed with noble intention" (āśayasampanna). Thus ends the *Yogimanoharā* commentary on the sequence of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*). There is no other jewel here than this self-consecration; because of its luminous purity, it is like a gem purified by fire.

Thus, considering that entry into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) is preceded by the objective support of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), [the author] says "having paid homage to Vajrasattva" and so forth, in order to demonstrate precisely that which is preceded by the salutation to the Great Vajradhara consisting of the four voids. He is called *Vajrasattva* because he is both a *vajra* and a *sattva*.
The connection is: "having paid homage to him whose form is the inseparable union of emptiness and compassion. Of what nature is he? One who teaches all voids (*sarvaśūnya*).
It is called the "Instruction on Universal Emptiness" because it teaches the supreme luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) which is entirely empty.

For this very reason, the fourth stage of manifest enlightenment (*abhisambodhikrama*) is the very form of Vajrasattva, whose nature consists of the four emptinesses. *Abhisambodhi* means "perfectly awakening" (*abhi* = everywhere, *samyak* = correctly) to the luminosity; the stage that establishes that is the "stage of manifest enlightenment," and thus it is the fourth.

It will be explained—that is, it will be spoken—by me, Nāgārjuna. Now he states the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of Vajrasattva and the Vajrācārya, beginning with the words "He is the Self-Arisen One" (*asau svayambhūḥ*).

Because he exists by himself through the thorough knowledge of all things as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), he is the Self-Arisen One; the Blessed One, the sole Vajrasattva, is the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) of the three realms. Therefore, the Vajrācārya is superior to that Vajrasattva. Why? Because of his bestowing of the oral instructions (*upadeśa*).

The commentary on the section beginning with "the propitiation of that" and ending with "the enjoyment of the five objects of desire" is easy to understand from the root text itself. Regarding the phrase "one should effect the arising of the light":
the Guru should effect the arising—that is, the experience—of the three knowledges, beginning with the light (*āloka*), within the ritual partner (*karmāṅganā*).

The meaning of the word "method" (*vidhāna*) is: "by means of the method of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), following the preliminary consecration of the vajra and lotus, through the union of the two organs.
Thus it is said in the *Anuttarasandhi*:
"Passion (*rāga*), dispassion (*virāga*), and that which is between the two—these three."

"From the union of the two organs, the meeting of the vajra and the lotus": this refers to the conventional bodhicitta. Having first carefully established it within a vessel and so forth by means of great effort, the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the lotus-vessel, the *sukatikā*, the conch, and other such items for the purpose of the secret initiation.
"One should consecrate at midnight," and so forth:

beginning from the onset of night until the end of the seven *ghaṭikās* of the night, having bestowed the master-consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*) and the secret-consecration (*guhyābhiṣeka*), one should then cause the experience of the two knowledges (*jñāna*) superior to that at the base of the *vajramaṇi*—namely, the knowledge of light (*āloka*) and so forth—and subsequently the wisdom-knowledge consecration (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*) should be bestowed. Furthermore, the fourth consecration is explained as being of the nature of the experience of these two; the "attainment of light" (*ālokopalabdha*) is the antidote to grasping at the wisdom-consecration.

The first interpretation explained is that the jewel born within the diamond-gem is the experience of great bliss, permeated by false habitual tendencies; whatever was taught by the Guru during the remainder of the third watch of the night is of the nature of direct experience.
Another section, distinct from the fourth initiation, is now described:

the fourth initiation is to be bestowed upon that wisdom (*prajñā*) in which the experience characterized by self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) has been explained. However, the knowledge of the experience of the fourth initiation occurs at the peak of the *vajramaṇi* (the jewel-tip) as the very third; how so? That which was established in the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) within the center of the jewel is to be contemplated at the tip of the jewel—the ineffable bliss, whose nature is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), the knowledge free from latent impressions (*nirvāsanajñāna*). This is the illustrative meaning of the fourth initiation.
And it is said in the *Sārdhaśataka*:
"Those faults, along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), do not exist in the one Protector.
The connection [of the verse] is that the Vajra-guru should consecrate the excellent disciple according to this sequence.
"Having obtained the consecration," and so forth:

having properly obtained the nature of the experience of the fourfold consecrations, the disciple— with palms joined— should worship and propitiate the Guru with the hymns to be mentioned later, such as "Liberated from the three realms," at the time of dawn— that is, again at the end of the night— specifically regarding the instruction on the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*), by means of the intrinsic nature of the Clear Light, according to the sequence to be described.

By the term "the three realms" (traidhātuka), there is the designation of the three types of luminous knowledge (*ālokajñāna*) which serve as the antidotes to the mind [perceiving] the grasped object and so forth. By means of this, one is liberated and devoid [of defilement], because its intrinsic nature is free from latent tendencies (*vāsana*);
for that very reason, having attained equality with space, you are not stained by sensual desires.
"You are not bound by craving;
you have emerged from objective support and conceptualization— you are without support," this is the word of address.
Homage be to you; homage be to you; let there be salutation to you whose state is without support.
Such a construction of words should also be inferred by the wise scholar in other verses, such as "unreliant" (*aniśrita*) and so forth.

Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), one should achieve thorough knowledge of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) by taking up the five aggregates beginning with form (*rūpa*) and extending to the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*), one should effect self-realization of the twelve bases by including those beginning with the eye base (*cakṣurāyatana*) and extending to the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Thus, because you possess a luminous nature (*prabhāsvara-svabhāva*), you are not dependent upon these [dharmas], nor do you rely on them;

for this very reason, you are free from error (*viparyāsa-vinirmukta*), non-conceptual (*avikalpita*), and so forth—devoid of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). That itself is true resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
He is one whose mind is non-abiding because its intrinsic nature is non-abiding;
for this very reason, his mental attention is inconceivable and his conceptualization is beyond thought.

Having praised [the Buddha] with the words beginning "anālayam" and ending with "śiṣyo gurum," as found in the root text, this is easy to understand. Immediately after the praise, he states the request to the Guru once again with the words beginning "prayaccha me mahānātha" and ending with "sadbhūtaguṇakīrttanaiḥ"; this too is clear.
Having generated compassion for the disciple, one should then begin this sequence;
that is, one should begin to explain the sequence of internal awakening by means of the sequence of manifest awakening.
First, the sequence of external awakening is described.
"The portion of night is light," and so forth:

the portion of night, whose nature is the wisdom of light, would be the intensely clear radiance of the sun; the appearance of light during the day has the nature of the means-knowledge (*upāyajñāna*).

The meaning is that these three cognitions— devoid of the light of day and possessing a form perceived during the twilight light— are joined with, or connected to, their own respective natures at all times,
not only during the portion of the night, and so forth.

The night, the day, and the portion of twilight have been shown through the cognitions of light and so forth as the antidotes to the apprehended object; however, this much does not constitute the threefold gnosis. Therefore, in response to the inquiry, "What then is the nature of luminosity (*prabhāsvara-svabhāva*)?", he says:

That which is "liberated by nature" (*prakṛti-vimukta*) refers to the triad of appearances and cognitions together with their nature; when these are abandoned and relinquished, what remains is that which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), designated as the fourth empowerment (*caturthābhiṣeka*), whose form is great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and whose characteristic is total emptiness (*sarvaśūnya*).
This would be the moment of awakening (*bodhikṣaṇa*) taught by the excellent Guru, accessible only to yogins. Regarding the phrase "naiśam" and so forth:
*naiśam* means the state of night (*niśi-bhāvam*); *naiśam* is derived from the suffix *-an* [denoting the abstract state].

The night darkness, which had vanished through the knowledge of light and so forth, and the gloom that had departed— when at that very moment all of it, including the twilight radiance, [is present], that [moment] is what must be described here;
is it, then, of the nature of twilight radiance?
In response to the doubt raised by the question, "Or is it something else entirely?", he states the refutation:
"This destroyed form has already been rejected by what preceded;
then, what specific moment is there that does not arise as radiant?"

This moment must be described here: in that stainless, pure moment which is the manifestation of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyaprabhāsa*), the preeminent teacher, the supreme Guru, should reveal the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) to the disciple. How is he characterized? He is "one whose darkness has been destroyed" (*vinihatatimira*). Darkness is precisely the triad of cognitions beginning with light; it is by this that [darkness] is removed. And this has been stated in the *Anuttarasandhi*:

"At the time of dawn, having sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree through the Vajropama-samādhi, he performed the crushing of Māra; having attained the unsurpassed knowledge of reality, the Lord of the Śākyas [did this] for the sake of the welfare of the three worlds—this very thing has been demonstrated here," and so forth, in detail.
"By the vision of external perfect enlightenment" means that one attains [it] through seeing, and so forth.

The sequence of internal awakening (*adhyātmasambodhi-krama*) is here described by one who has accomplished the realization of bliss: first, a single cognition in the form of a mirage arises; subsequently, the three cognitions of light arise in succession. This quartet of cognitions, together with their latent predispositions (*savāsana*), is of the nature of darkness. When that [darkness] is removed, at the fourth moment—the moment of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) taught by the Guru—the disciple attains through that very moment the awakening (*bodhi*) and Buddhahood (*buddhatva*) of a Buddha.

Of what nature is Buddhahood? It is internal bliss, consisting of the experience of the aspect of coolness (*śātākāra*), characterized by universal emptiness, free from turbidity, and devoid of afflictions; this very state is also described as having the nature of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Thus it is said in the *Sūtaka*:
"First, one should see the form of a mirage, a mass of five-colored rays."
The second [vision] is light, resembling moonbeams; the third is the appearance of light, resembling sunbeams;

the fourth has the form of darkness, wherein light is perceived. Then, when that darkness has vanished in an instant, one should behold with the eye of gnosis (jñānacakṣus) the supreme radiance—extremely pure, having the nature of constant light, and characterized by ultimate reality (paramārthasatya). Now, he states the essential nature of the luminosity (prabhāsvara) thus established, beginning with "anādibhūtam" and so forth.

Since this nature of phenomena (dharmatā) of these phenomena remains constant, the stage of union (yuganaddhakrama)— which is beginningless and, through the process of luminosity (prabhāsvara), becomes the end— becomes the middle-less foundation (amadhyabhūta).
Self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna) is the beginning, and the stage of union is the end.

Between these two, it is said that "luminosity" (*prabhāsvara*) abides; thus it is the intermediate state. Because it is the very essence of all Buddhas, the stage of union (*yuganaddha-krama*) is the infinite state. Having effected the removal of conceptual construction regarding the three gnoses, luminosity—which is characterized as the fourth consecration—is the final state. This is what is expressed in this verse.
Alternatively, these three words function with respect to three meanings, namely, within the internal operations of alternative positions regarding the meaning;
thus, the wise and virtuous proclaim that all this is empty for such knowledge,
and he now states the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this very knowledge.
Regarding "going and not going," and so forth:
since form is unarisen from the very beginning, the conventional designations of "going" and "not going" are impossible;
this is a state of extreme wonder.
Because its intrinsic nature is the *dharmakāya*,
there is no persistence [of it], according to the statement: "The various powers of entities are beyond wonder."
It does not abide in a single place because it is all-pervasive,
nor is it mobile;
this is clear from the previous explanation.

Regarding the passage beginning with "that which exists" (*yad asti*): that non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) which exists is free from and has abandoned the conventional usage of non-existence (*nāstitva-vyavahāra*).
How then is existence and non-existence manifested therein? This is stated [as follows] according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
In such phrases as "not of the nature of merit," this kind of explanation is to be understood by the yogin: here, [the reality] is real because it is devoid of both sin and merit.
Is that then a universal void?
The Buddhas, the perfectly awakened ones, declare that this gnosis, whose intrinsic nature is suchness endowed with the excellence of all aspects, is the "all-empty" (sarvaśūnya);
thus it is said in the Āgama.
But those who perceive suchness by following the meaning of the Middle Way—they are indeed the fortunate knowers of reality, provided they have direct personal experience through their own awareness.
Indeed, no superimposition whatsoever is capable in any way; for the meaning of the Middle Way is free from superimposition—how, then, could there be negation or affirmation therein?
"Thus," and so forth:

having attained—that is, having reached—such a reality (tattva) which is of the nature of non-arising, [he is] the self of all things, both moving and unmoving, that is, the self of all entities whether stationary or mobile, because of his state of being of a single flavor (ekarasa).
He is the sole kinsman of the world.
Because its intrinsic nature is non-referential compassion (*nirālambana-karuṇā*),
the yogin— who consists of gnosis and is Nṛsiṃha— wanders and roams throughout the entire world in its totality. He becomes one who has attained the imperishable and undecaying body.
"He has a crooked body," and so forth; [this refers to] being sluggish due to the power of suchness (*tathatā*),
whereas he has a straight body because he is engaged in acting for the sake of sentient beings, impelled by compassion (*karuṇā*).
He is "without a seat" because of the absence of any fixed seat.
He is "steadfast in the binding of the seat," yet no binding occurs upon the seat because its intrinsic nature is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
With eyes closed, because he is motionless through the power of emptiness; with eyes wide open, because of his excessive joy;
and being in meditative equipoise, because he gazes upon suchness.
He is not unconcentrated, because he discerns all phenomena through their nature as suchness (*tathatā*).
He is restrained in speech, because he is established solely in emptiness. He is endowed with discourse, because he acts for the benefit of sentient beings.
He is endowed with enjoyments, because he has obtained the causes for excellence both mundane and supramundane.
He is one whose conduct is free from deformity, because he is averse to the eight worldly dharmas.
He is the protector of the world, because he has awakened to the suchness of the Buddhas.

He has become a servant to others because of the absence of pride. He is the yogin who knows reality, whose all faults have been exhausted, and who has received the instructions; such is the disciple, and so forth.
One should focus on the two-fold meditation by means of this sequence:
first by the method of grasping as a whole (*piṇḍagrāha*), and likewise by the subsequent analysis (*anubheda*).
Grasping the body as a whole—that is, as empty—is "grasping as a whole."

Its sequence is therefore exactly like that; subsequently, the division and sub-division—the sequence for grasping the whole—is first described by the verse beginning with "from the head or from the feet."
One should practice the sequence of penetration (*anubhedakrama*); therein, this is the sequence:

having first rendered both the stationary (*sthāvaram*) and the moving (*jaṅgamam*) luminous (*prabhāsvara*), according to the instruction, "the drop (*bindu*) which is dissolved in pure water, in a river or a lake," one should subsequently make even oneself of the nature of luminosity (*prabhāsvarasvabhāva*). This sequence of penetration has indeed been written down.
In this regard, a doubt should be considered: should the experience of the apprehension of a mass (*piṇḍagraha*) be practiced by a single yogin, or rather by one who is distinct [from that]?
To this, the response is stated:
The dissolution of the grasping at a solid mass is to be practiced;
between these two, whichever yoga one desires, that one should practice. How is it to be undertaken?
For this purpose, he provides an illustration.

The word-by-word construction (*padayojanā*) of the verse beginning with "Just as the breath-wind dissolves everywhere into a mirror" has not been provided from the root text because it is already extremely clear.

And it was said by the venerable Āryadeva in the *Sūtaka*: "Just as a drop that has dissolved into pure water in a river or a lake, in that same way the yogi should constantly recollect in sequence what was taught regarding the successive dissolution;
for in a mirror, the destruction of the wind occurs through a gradual process."
In the same way, the sequence of grasping the [bodily] mass (piṇḍagrāha) is to be visualized by those who follow the ritual rules;
thus, from "while walking" up to "the knower of reality," it is very easy to understand from the root text itself.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the welfare of sentient beings might also sometimes occur," and so forth:

Even when acting for the benefit of sentient beings, by means of rays corresponding to each [specific purpose], one accomplishes all four types of ritual action—such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth—through the process of immediate self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) by way of the nature of Vajrasattva endowed with five rays;
the word "tu" serves to complete the meter.
To illustrate this point, he states an analogy:
By this verse beginning with "Just as from the clear water of a river," the method of simultaneous union (*yuganaddha-krama*) was indeed established by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna.
He speaks again of this very same deity-form consisting of emergence in the words "dependent on the five Buddha-families," and so forth;
that Great Seal (mahāmudrā) upon which the five Buddha-families depend is described as such.
The form of the deity composed of the five gnoses, such as the mirror-like wisdom and so forth, is Mahāmudrā; moreover, that is the embodiment of the Great Vajradhara.
For this very reason, Mahāmudrā possesses sovereignty over the five Buddhas.
In this sense, resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) is what is expressed by the term "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*).
But no other conceptual construction remains;
one simply experiences the body of the distinguished deity through the form of the path of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) to this extent,
and so it has been said:
Because of the statement, "The path is the union (yuganaddha), and the fruit is the union," by the word "etcetera" (ādi) there is the inclusion of the action-mudrās and the pledge-mudrās,
which arise from the five rays of light.
The Great Seal (mahāmudrā), endowed with rays of five colors, would arise; having arisen,
where in the sky does it abide?
Who,
like a rainbow,
joining all things together through this single nature, says:
The explanation of the passage beginning with "the binding of the mudrās" and ending with "is purified by the all-empty" is now stated:

the collective meaning of the sentence is explained as follows—that everything is purified by means of the "all-empty," which is being meditated upon as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), in the form of the abandonment of the obscurations of all conceptual constructions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
[This applies to] the fortunate and excellent disciple who has received the instruction, and so forth.
For since the mind is indeed directed toward awakening (*bodhi*), it is called "awakening-mind" (*bodhicitta*); this is the designation for ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Furthermore, with palms joined and holding flowers in his hands, [he receives it] from this Guru.
This is a form of the *liṅ* (optative) mood; therefore, how is it to be understood?

To this end, the commentary is introduced according to the sequence of the preceding text: "Previously, that which was described by the Guru as 'special knowledge' (*viśiṣṭajñāna*)—to be designated as the fourth moment within the lotus of wisdom (*prajñāravinda*)—must now be grasped by means of its verbal expression alone. Thus, the good disciple, having mastered its pervasion (*vyāpti*), should correctly receive the instruction regarding the essential meaning (*piṇḍārtha*)," and so forth.

"Free from all entities" means it is free from all entities; that which is devoid of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, as well as the grasped and the grasper, should be known by the practitioner of the highest-of-the-high degree as the nature of self-reflexive awareness through the equality of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), just like the phenomena of trees, mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth.

The excellent guru demonstrates to the disciple that, because their intrinsic nature is primordially unarisen, the *tathatā*s (suchnesses) have the nature of emptiness; likewise, one's own mind is primordially unarisen and has the nature of emptiness.

Thus, this has been explained: for one who is devoted to the noble and profound method, one should give the jewel of consecration by means of speech alone; the meaning of this has been shown, and furthermore, the reality is that what is designated by the term "the fourth consecration" is also called innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). This is the truth.
"Then," and so forth;
therefore, one should give a fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru according to what is appropriate,
such as a jewel, and so on.

"What else remains?"—up to this point, it is easy to understand. Having attained knowledge, he describes the nature of its fruit with the words "having obtained the grace of the teacher," and so forth;
"obtained" means that the instruction on reality has been received.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "one whose mind is firm, stainless, and pure through the grace of the teacher (ācārya) and the grace of the guru.
The connection is that the yogin, established on the path of reality, should meditate upon—that is, directly realize—reality (tattva).
Of what nature is the yogi of reality?
Reality, which is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, is of what nature? It is translucent.
Because it is non-obstructive in nature;
it is pure because it is free from the two kinds of obscurations.
It is extremely subtle because it is difficult to perceive; it consists of supreme bliss because it brings about auspiciousness.
It is the *dhātu*—the element—because it sustains (*dadhāti*) the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, which is liberation; thus it is the "Buddha-nirvāṇa-element," free from all duality.
Because it is devoid of both existence and nirvāṇa;
it is non-conceptual because it transcends all conceptual constructions.

It consists of constant bliss, because it is by nature the experience of a state of peace at all times. The yogi who has directly realized reality is liberated from, that is, devoid of, both merit and demerit.
It is established that by personally engaging in the cultivation of reality here, one becomes the Blessed One Vajrasattva; one comes to possess the very nature of the vajra.
Regarding the sequence of the realization of the supreme secret bliss:
it is both supreme and secret;
and it is both bliss and realization.
And because it is both the supreme secret and the clear realization of bliss,
it is the "Supreme Secret Clear Realization of Bliss";
[it is] the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), and its sequence is the *krama*.
Thus ends the *Yogimanoharā* commentary on the *Prabhāsvarakrama*. May there be success!

Out of the intention to benefit sentient beings and by the power of his previous vows, [the author], after rising from the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*) through the process of simultaneous union (*yuganaddha-krama*) and preceded by an act of homage, speaks the following—beginning with "consisting of cause and fruit"—in order to demonstrate that very [union]. The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "Having bowed down—that is, having prostrated—to the Protector who has become the refuge of the worlds, the supreme process of simultaneous union (*yuganaddha-kramottama*), whose meaning is correctly ascertained, is now being written. Of what nature is this Protector? He is "consisting of cause and fruit" (*phalahetvātmaka*). The "fruit" is the Clear Light; the "cause" is the illusory body (*māyādeha*), which is designated by the term "self-consecration" (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). The unity of these two is "consisting of cause and fruit," which is simultaneous union (*yuganaddha*). For this very reason, he is "devoid of all dualities. The "supreme process of simultaneous union": having known the Clear Light through the intellect and having realized it, one who knows—that is, understands—their unification, [perceives] "the conceptualization of form and non-existence," and so forth. The conceptualization of existence with form is self-consecration; the conceptualization of formlessness is the Clear Light. Having unified these two, one should practice—that is, one should engage in worldly activity.

The yogi knows—that is, he understands—the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*), and so forth. The apprehended is the clear light (*prabhāsvara*); the apprehender is the impure illusory body (*māyādeha*). Wherein there is non-duality—that is, where cognition does not exist or arise in a dual manner—he speaks of that as "one should cultivate non-differentiation. Regarding the phrase "the cognitions of permanence and annihilation," and so forth: "permanence" is the impure illusory body; "annihilation" is the clear light. Furthermore, the unity of wisdom (*prajñā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) is mentioned: wisdom is the clear light; compassion is the pure illusory body. "The union of wisdom and means": wisdom is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); means is the illusory body. Wherein there is both the *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and the *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder), and so forth: the *sopadhiśeṣa* is the illusory body; the *nirupadhiśeṣa* is nirvāṇa. Wherein there is the selflessness of the person (*pudgalanairātmya*), and so forth: the selflessness of the person is the form of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*); having known the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) as the clear light, and so forth. The passage ending with "the yogi’s immutable state" is easy to understand. Regarding "asleep and awakened," and so forth: this excludes the two states. The state of sleep is the clear light; the state of being awakened is the illusory body. Regarding "concentration and non-concentration," and so forth: concentration is the clear light; non-concentration is the illusory body. Regarding "freed from non-recollection and recollection," and so forth: non-recollection is the clear light; recollection is the illusory body. Regarding "freed from passion and dispassion," and so forth: passion is the illusory body; dispassion is the clear light. Regarding "effect and cause," and so forth: the effect is the clear light; the cause is the illusory body. Regarding the passage beginning with "this is one stage of the generation process (*utpattikrama*)" and ending with "like a drop of water on the Gaṅgā," among these there are words expressing conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and words expressing ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Having understood the unity of these two, the wise should perform the proclamation of synonyms for the nature of the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*) according to the sequence described.
"Striving," and so forth: striving, that is, exerting himself, the great yogin established in the state of union (*yuganaddha*) should cultivate union.

"And the conduct following that" means he should perform the conduct that is utterly free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); this is the remainder [of the sense]. Here, however, there is a specific instruction.

Indeed, the practice that is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and utterly free from conceptual proliferation has been explained in the *Piṇḍīkrama*; therefore, it is not mentioned here. And it is said in the *Sūtaka*: "One burns wood and there is ash; one burns a palm leaf and there is ash; one burns cotton and there is ash. To show that the practice should be performed with the sense of a single nature (*ekasvabhāva*) everywhere, he says: "Just as in oneself," and so forth, up to "all perfections are accomplished. This is easy to understand from the root text itself. This too is stated in the *Sūtaka*: "The yogi, whose doubts are severed in every respect, should conduct himself like a child; when the yogi is without effort (*nirābhoga*), then perfections rain down."

And it is said in the *Śrīsamāja-ṭīkā*: "Through the union of the vajra and the lotus, one who discerns the three types of gnosis should always dwell there with ease, whether his mind is defiled or undefiled."

Even having performed what is forbidden, one who knows the true nature of reality and is free from the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done is not defiled, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
The commentary on the verse ending with "having made merit manifest" is even clearer.
Thus ends the *Yogimanoharā* commentary on the sequence of the Union (*yuganaddha*).

Having bowed to my gurus and the Triple Refuge—the majestic mountain that serves as a base for the ocean of the profound methods of mantra, which is difficult to attain and far-reaching—and having performed this analysis of the Five Stages, may whatever merit I have gained lead all beings to the attainment of supreme enlightenment.

This commentary, which acts as a bee upon the pair of his lotus feet, was composed by the venerable monk Śrī Bhadra—a bee among the great monastic community of the world—for a long time, after he had propitiated many gurus; it was produced through the power of wisdom and the inspiration of the greatness of the foremost lineages of disciples and teachers, and is charming to the wise by its name.

One who is devoted to grasping the vital points of others' virtues does not speak of the multitude of others' faults; for even the nectar-like abundance of the wise's virtues is obscured by the ignorant, who perceive only the creepers of their faults.
This work is the composition of the scholar from the land of Magadha, the Śākya bhikṣu Muniśrībhadra.
Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
May all virtue be auspicious.
